title: Taxonomic composition and guilds
text:
Which fungi dominate the communities, and how does the composition change between land uses? Taxa plots (stacked bar plots) show the relative abundance of the most abundant taxa in each site or group of samples. Grouping the fungi by their lifestyle (e.g., saprotrophs, mycorrhizal fungi, pathogens) helps to interpret these changes ecologically. Both are descriptive: they do not test whether the differences are significant (see Beta diversity and Indicator species for statistical tests).
This section documents how to find the dominant OTUs, how to draw taxa plots at different taxonomic ranks, and how to assign fungal lifestyles with the FungalTraits database[1]. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 040_taxa_composition.R, the example data and the FungalTraits table by clicking the buttons below. Save the FungalTraits table in the folder raw data/. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.
Download script


 


 Download example RData


 


 Download FungalTraits
To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see BLAST filtering), and set the seed for the rarefaction.
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
set.seed(100)

title: Taxonomic composition and guilds
text:
Rarefaction and relative abundances
As in Alpha diversity, we start from the data rarefied to 1011 reads (same seed, so the same rarefied table). All samples then have the same number of reads.

otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, sample.size = 1011,
                                      replace = FALSE, rngseed = 100,
                                      verbose = FALSE)
nsamples(otu_table_rarefy)

[1] 87

ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)

[1] 5153


Taxa plots show relative abundances: the proportion of the reads of a sample that belong to an OTU or a taxon.

otu_table_rel <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_rarefy, function(x) x / sum(x))

# Check: the relative abundances of each sample should sum to 1
head(sample_sums(otu_table_rel))

SNF4__29367 SNF4__29368 SNF4__29369 SNF4__29370 SNF4__29371 SNF4__29372 
          1           1           1           1           1           1 



Long format table
To summarise and plot the relative abundances with dplyr and ggplot2, we convert the phyloseq object to a long format table (one row per OTU and per sample) with phyloseq::psmelt(). The tax_table contains 37 columns (taxonomy and BLAST results). To keep the long table small, we only keep the taxonomic ranks. OTUs without a confident assignment at a given rank were changed to NA in BLAST filtering; we rename them “Unassigned” to show them in the plots.

tax_table(otu_table_rel) <- tax_table(otu_table_rel)[, c("phylum", "class",
                                                         "order", "family",
                                                         "genus", "species")]

rel_long <- psmelt(otu_table_rel) %>%
  select(OTU, Sample, SiteID, Land_use, Abundance,
         phylum, class, order, family, genus, species) %>%
  mutate(across(phylum:species, ~ if_else(is.na(.x) | .x == "NA",
                                          "Unassigned", .x)))

# Order the sites by land use for the plots
rel_long$SiteID <- factor(rel_long$SiteID,
                          levels = unique(rel_long$SiteID[order(rel_long$Land_use,
                                                                rel_long$SiteID)]))







Note



psmelt() keeps the OTUs with an abundance of 0. This is important when calculating means: an OTU absent from a sample must count as 0 in the mean, not be ignored.

Dominant OTUs
Which OTUs dominate the fungal communities of each site? We calculate the mean relative abundance of each OTU across the samples of a site, and show the 10 most abundant OTUs of the organic agriculture site and of the old oak forest (reference site).

  group_by(SiteID, Land_use, OTU, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species) %>%
  summarise(mean_relab = mean(Abundance), .groups = "drop")

# The 10 most abundant OTUs in the organic agriculture site...
otu_mean %>%
  filter(SiteID == "Org_agri") %>%
  slice_max(mean_relab, n = 10) %>%

The dominant OTUs differ between the two sites. In the agricultural site, the most abundant OTUs belong to typical soil saprotrophs and yeasts (e.g., Plectosphaerellaceae, Mortierella, Solicoccozyma). In the old oak forest, ectomycorrhizal genera such as Russula and Inocybe, which live in symbiosis with the roots of oaks, are among the dominant OTUs. Even the most abundant OTUs represent only a few percent of the reads, and many of them cannot be assigned to a genus. Try other sites by changing the SiteID in the code above.

title: Taxonomic composition and guilds
text:
Taxa plots
There are too many taxa to give each of them a colour, especially at low taxonomic ranks (e.g., genus). We therefore show only the most abundant taxa, and group all other taxa into “Other”. OTUs without a confident assignment at the chosen rank are shown as “Unassigned”.

# How many taxa are there at each rank?
rel_long %>% summarise(across(phylum:genus, n_distinct))

  phylum class order family genus
1     20    70   167    317   585


The steps are the same for every taxonomic rank, so we write them in two functions. taxa_site() summarises the relative abundances at a chosen rank and returns the mean relative abundance of each taxon per site:

data: the long format table
rank: the taxonomic rank to summarise (e.g., "phylum")
n_taxa: the number of most abundant taxa to show


taxa_site <- function(data, rank, n_taxa) {
  # 1. Sum the relative abundances of all OTUs of a taxon, in each sample
  taxa_sample <- data %>%
    group_by(Sample, SiteID, Land_use, taxon = .data[[rank]]) %>%
    summarise(Abundance = sum(Abundance), .groups = "drop")

  # 2. Find the n most abundant taxa (mean across all samples)
  top_taxa <- taxa_sample %>%
    filter(taxon != "Unassigned") %>%
    group_by(taxon) %>%
    summarise(mean_relab = mean(Abundance)) %>%
    slice_max(mean_relab, n = n_taxa) %>%
    pull(taxon)

  # 3. Group all other taxa into "Other", then calculate the mean per site
  taxa_sample %>%
    mutate(taxon = if_else(taxon %in% c(top_taxa, "Unassigned"), taxon, "Other")) %>%
    group_by(Sample, SiteID, Land_use, taxon) %>%
    summarise(Abundance = sum(Abundance), .groups = "drop") %>%
    group_by(SiteID, Land_use, taxon) %>%
    summarise(Abundance = mean(Abundance), .groups = "drop") %>%
    # Order the taxa from most to least abundant, followed by Other and Unassigned
    mutate(taxon = factor(taxon, levels = c(top_taxa, "Other", "Unassigned")))
}

plot_taxa() draws the stacked bar plot, with one panel per land use. Colours are interpolated from the RColorBrewer palette “Set3” (12 colours), so that any number of taxa can be shown. “Other” and “Unassigned” are shown in grey.

taxa_df: the table returned by taxa_site()
legend_title: the title of the legend (e.g., "Phylum")


plot_taxa <- function(taxa_df, legend_title) {
  n_top <- nlevels(taxa_df$taxon) - 2
  colours <- c(colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(12, "Set3"))(n_top),
               "grey60", "grey85")
  names(colours) <- levels(taxa_df$taxon)

  ggplot(taxa_df, aes(x = SiteID, y = Abundance, fill = taxon)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colours, name = legend_title) +
    # One panel per land use, with the panel width proportional to the
    # number of sites
    facet_grid(~ Land_use, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x",
               labeller = label_wrap_gen(width = 12)) +
    ylab("Mean relative abundance") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
}


Phylum

phylum_site <- taxa_site(rel_long, rank = "phylum", n_taxa = 10)

# Check: the relative abundances of each site should sum to 1
phylum_site %>% group_by(SiteID) %>% summarise(total = sum(Abundance))

# A tibble: 10 × 2
   SiteID    total
   <fct>     <dbl>
 1 Conv_agri     1
 2 Grass         1
 3 Oak_20        1
 4 Oak_28        1
 5 Oak_33        1
 6 Oak_44        1
 7 Oak_51        1
 8 Oak_54        1
 9 Oak_ref       1
10 Org_agri      1

plot_taxa(phylum_site, "Phylum")








Ascomycota and Basidiomycota dominate in all sites, as is common in soils. Ascomycota dominate in the agricultural sites and the grassland (46-62% of the reads), Basidiomycota in the oak forests (~60%), where many of them are ectomycorrhizal (see the guilds below). Mortierellomycota are more abundant in the agricultural sites (14-21%) than in the forests (6-8%).


Genus

genus_site <- taxa_site(rel_long, rank = "genus", n_taxa = 20)
plot_taxa(genus_site, "Genus")








At the genus level, 17% (Oak_20) to 50% (Conv_agri) of the reads are unassigned: many soil fungi have not been described, or their ITS sequences are too different from the reference sequences to be assigned to a genus with confidence (see the rank-level thresholds in BLAST filtering). The 20 most abundant genera represent only a small part of the community.






Tip



It is common to remove the unassigned reads and to rescale the top taxa to 100%. This makes the plot easier to read, but it hides how little of the community is actually shown. If you do so, always state it in the figure legend.




Variation between samples
The site means hide the variation between the samples of the same site. microViz::comp_barplot() draws one bar per sample. It calculates the relative abundances itself, so we give it the rarefied counts. We first keep only the taxonomic ranks in the tax_table (comp_barplot() would treat the BLAST columns as taxonomic ranks). tax_fix() replaces the unassigned ranks (NA) with the name of the closest assigned rank above it (e.g., “Fungi Kingdom”), which comp_barplot() requires.

otu_table_ranks <- otu_table_rarefy
tax_table(otu_table_ranks) <- tax_table(otu_table_ranks)[, c("kingdom", "phylum",
                                                             "class", "order",
                                                             "family", "genus")]

# Each panel is a site, each bar is a sample
otu_table_ranks %>%
  tax_fix() %>%
  comp_barplot(tax_level = "phylum", n_taxa = 10, facet_by = "SiteID",
               bar_width = 0.9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())








The samples of the same site have a similar composition, but the variation between samples can be large: in Oak_28, for example, Basidiomycota make up 35% to 90% of the reads of a sample.

title: Taxonomic composition and guilds
text:
Fungal guilds and lifestyles
Fungi have very different ecological roles in soil: decomposers (saprotrophs), mycorrhizal symbionts (e.g., ectomycorrhizal fungi associated with oaks, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi associated with grasses and most crops), and pathogens of plants or animals. Grouping fungi by their lifestyle or trophic mode (how they obtain nutrients) helps to interpret the changes in the communities. The three trophic modes are:

Saprotroph: feeds on dead organic matter.
Symbiotroph: obtains nutrients by exchanging resources with a host (e.g., mycorrhizal fungi, lichens, endophytes).
Pathotroph: obtains nutrients by harming a host (pathogens, parasites).

The most up-to-date database of fungal lifestyles is FungalTraits[1], which gives the primary and secondary lifestyle of more than 10,000 fungal genera.






WarningPotential functions




The ecology of most fungi is only known from observational (correlative) studies.
Many fungi switch between strategies, e.g., an endophyte can become a pathogen or a saprotroph.
The assignments are potential functions: the actual function can vary with the environment, the geography or the host.
The assignments are made at the genus level, as most functional traits of fungi are conserved within genera (and the species hypotheses of UNITE[2] are not species). Only OTUs assigned to a genus can be assigned to a lifestyle, and in soil a large part of the fungal OTUs cannot be assigned to a genus.




Load the FungalTraits database
FungalTraits is distributed as a table (supplementary material of the paper). We use version 1.2 (16 Dec 2020), as distributed with the R package microeco, saved as a .csv file in the folder raw data/ (download it with the button at the top of this page). It has one row per genus.

fungal_traits <- read.csv("raw data/FungalTraits_1.2.csv")

None of them is in our data, but a duplicated genus would duplicate OTUs in the join below, so we keep the first row of each genus. The lifestyle of many genera is not known (empty primary_lifestyle): we replace the empty values by NA, so that these genera are treated like the genera that are not in the database.

[1] 1321

fungal_traits <- fungal_traits %>%
  mutate(primary_lifestyle = na_if(primary_lifestyle, ""))



Trophic modes
FungalTraits gives detailed lifestyles, which we group into the three trophic modes. Lifestyles that do not fit any of the three (e.g., “unspecified”, “bacterivorous”) are grouped into “Other”. Genera without a lifestyle (NA) stay NA.

lifestyle_to_trophic <- function(x) {
  case_when(
    is.na(x) ~ NA_character_,
    grepl("saprotroph|sooty_mold", x) ~ "Saprotroph",
    grepl("mycorrhizal|endophyte|lichenized|epiphyte|symbiont|symbiotroph", x) ~ "Symbiotroph",
    grepl("pathogen|parasite|pathotroph", x) ~ "Pathotroph",
    TRUE ~ "Other")
}

# Check the grouping: which trophic mode was given to each lifestyle?
fungal_traits %>%
  filter(!is.na(primary_lifestyle)) %>%
  distinct(primary_lifestyle) %>%
  mutate(trophic_mode = lifestyle_to_trophic(primary_lifestyle)) %>%
  arrange(trophic_mode)

Add the lifestyles to the taxonomy table
We extract the taxonomy table, and join the FungalTraits columns that we need by genus. Unassigned genera (NA) do not match any genus of the database.






Note



The genus names must be written the same way in both tables (here, e.g., “Russula”). Some taxonomy tables add prefixes such as “g__Russula”: remove them before the join.



tax_traits <- as.data.frame(tax_table(otu_table_rarefy)) %>%
  select(taxa_OTU, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species) %>%
  left_join(fungal_traits %>%
              select(GENUS, primary_lifestyle, Secondary_lifestyle),
            by = c("genus" = "GENUS"))

# Check: the number of rows has not changed (one row per OTU)
nrow(tax_traits) == ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)

[1] TRUE


A genus can have a second lifestyle with another trophic mode. For each trophic mode, we note whether the primary or the secondary lifestyle belongs to it.

tax_traits <- tax_traits %>%
  mutate(
    # Genera without a secondary lifestyle ("") become "none"
    Secondary_lifestyle = case_when(is.na(primary_lifestyle) ~ NA_character_,
                                    Secondary_lifestyle == "" ~ "none",
                                    TRUE ~ Secondary_lifestyle),
    # Primary trophic mode, from the primary lifestyle
    primary_trophic = lifestyle_to_trophic(primary_lifestyle),
    # Can the OTU act as each trophic mode (primary or secondary lifestyle)?
    Symbiotroph = if_else(lifestyle_to_trophic(primary_lifestyle) == "Symbiotroph" |
                            lifestyle_to_trophic(Secondary_lifestyle) == "Symbiotroph",
                          "yes", "no"),
    Pathotroph = if_else(lifestyle_to_trophic(primary_lifestyle) == "Pathotroph" |
                           lifestyle_to_trophic(Secondary_lifestyle) == "Pathotroph",
                         "yes", "no"),
    Saprotroph = if_else(lifestyle_to_trophic(primary_lifestyle) == "Saprotroph" |
                           lifestyle_to_trophic(Secondary_lifestyle) == "Saprotroph",
                         "yes", "no"),
    # OTUs with traits (genus found in FungalTraits)
    traits = if_else(is.na(primary_lifestyle), "no", "yes"))

# How many OTUs have traits?
table(tax_traits$traits)


  no  yes 
3109 2044 

# Percentage of OTUs without traits
mean(tax_traits$traits == "no") * 100

[1] 60.33379

# How many of the OTUs with traits can act as each trophic mode?
tax_traits %>%
  filter(traits == "yes") %>%
  summarise(Symb = sum(Symbiotroph == "yes"),
            Pat = sum(Pathotroph == "yes"),
            Sap = sum(Saprotroph == "yes"))

  Symb Pat  Sap
1  680 496 1431


Only 2044 of the 5153 OTUs (40%) could be assigned to a lifestyle: the others are not assigned to a genus, or the lifestyle of their genus is unknown. An OTU can be counted in two trophic modes (primary and secondary lifestyles).






Note



In the course tutorial, a pre-processed traits table assigns traits to slightly more OTUs (43%), because the OTUs were matched to FungalTraits differently. More generally, the low proportion of OTUs with traits is due to the few OTUs identified at the genus level. It could be improved by revising the BLAST results, e.g., by checking the uncertain OTUs manually (see BLAST filtering).




Relative abundance of the trophic modes and lifestyles
We join the traits to the long format table. OTUs without traits are labelled “No traits”, so that the bars show which part of the community could be assigned.

traits_long <- rel_long %>%
  select(OTU, Sample, SiteID, Land_use, Abundance) %>%
  left_join(tax_traits %>%
              select(taxa_OTU, primary_trophic, primary_lifestyle,
                     Secondary_lifestyle),
            by = c("OTU" = "taxa_OTU")) %>%
  mutate(across(primary_trophic:Secondary_lifestyle,
                ~ if_else(is.na(.x), "No traits", .x)))

As in the course tutorial, we average the samples per land use. The Oak land use pools the samples of the six oak forests of different ages (see the taxa plots above for the individual sites). trait_landuse() sums the relative abundances per trait in each sample, then calculates the mean per land use (in %); plot_traits() draws the stacked bar plot, with “No traits” in grey.

trait_landuse <- function(data, trait) {
  trait_df <- data %>%
    group_by(Sample, Land_use, trait = .data[[trait]]) %>%
    summarise(Abundance = sum(Abundance), .groups = "drop") %>%
    group_by(Land_use, trait) %>%
    summarise(Mean_Rel_Abundance = mean(Abundance) * 100, .groups = "drop")

  # Order the traits from most to least abundant, with "No traits" last
  trait_order <- trait_df %>%
    filter(trait != "No traits") %>%
    group_by(trait) %>%
    summarise(total = sum(Mean_Rel_Abundance)) %>%
    arrange(desc(total)) %>%
    pull(trait)
  trait_df %>%
    mutate(trait = factor(trait, levels = c(trait_order, "No traits")))
}

plot_traits <- function(trait_df, legend_title) {
  n_traits <- nlevels(trait_df$trait) - 1
  colours <- c(colorRampPalette(brewer.pal(12, "Set3"))(n_traits), "grey85")
  names(colours) <- levels(trait_df$trait)

  ggplot(trait_df, aes(x = Land_use, y = Mean_Rel_Abundance, fill = trait)) +
    geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.7) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colours, name = legend_title) +
    labs(x = "Land use", y = "Mean relative abundance (%)") +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}


Primary trophic mode

trophic_landuse <- trait_landuse(traits_long, "primary_trophic")
plot_traits(trophic_landuse, "Primary trophic mode")








21% (Oak) to 50% (conventional agriculture) of the reads belong to OTUs without traits. Among the others, saprotrophs dominate in the agricultural sites and the grassland (41-50% of the reads), where symbiotrophs are almost absent (~1%). In the oak forests, symbiotrophs are the largest group (47% in the oak plantations, 17% in the old reference forest). Pathotrophs represent 5-11% of the reads in all land uses.


Primary lifestyle

primary_landuse <- trait_landuse(traits_long, "primary_lifestyle")
plot_traits(primary_landuse, "Primary lifestyle")








The primary lifestyles show which symbionts these are: almost all are ectomycorrhizal fungi, which live with the roots of the oaks, and are absent from the open land uses (< 0.1%). Soil saprotrophs dominate in the agricultural sites and the grassland. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (Glomeromycota) are rare everywhere (< 1%), although grasses and most crops are their hosts: they are poorly amplified by the common ITS primers, so their abundance is underestimated. Use specific primers (e.g., for the 18S rRNA gene) to study them.


Secondary lifestyle
Fungi can have more than one lifestyle. The database also describes a secondary lifestyle (“none” if the genus has only one lifestyle).

secondary_landuse <- trait_landuse(traits_long, "Secondary_lifestyle")
plot_traits(secondary_landuse, "Secondary lifestyle")








In the agricultural sites, many saprotrophs are also root-associated or foliar endophytes, i.e. they can live inside living plants.






Important



As for alpha diversity, the land uses are not replicated (one site per land use, except for the oak forests). Use these plots to describe patterns, not to test differences between land uses with the samples as replicates.

title: Taxonomic composition and guilds

Exercises

title: Indicator species
text:
Beta diversity showed that the fungal communities differ between land uses. Which OTUs are responsible for these differences? Several methods can identify OTUs associated with a group of samples. This section documents two of them:
To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 030_diff_abund.R and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.
Download script


 


 Download example RData
To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see BLAST filtering), and set the seed for the rarefaction and the permutation tests. We also order the land uses from agriculture to the old forest, and define their colours for the plots.
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
set.seed(100)

sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use <- factor(
  sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use,
  levels = c("Conventional agriculture", "Organic agriculture", "Grassland",
             "Oak", "Old Ref"))

land_use_col <- c("Conventional agriculture" = "bisque",
                  "Organic agriculture" = "bisque3",
                  "Grassland" = "orange",
                  "Oak" = "darkolivegreen2",
                  "Old Ref" = "turquoise4")

Data preparation
As in Alpha diversity and Beta diversity, we start from the data rarefied to 1011 reads (same seed, so the same rarefied table).

otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, sample.size = 1011,
                                      replace = FALSE, rngseed = 100,
                                      verbose = FALSE)
nsamples(otu_table_rarefy)

ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)

indicspecies and mvabund do not work with phyloseq objects: they need the OTU table as a matrix with the samples as rows and the OTUs as columns. In our phyloseq object the OTUs are the rows (taxa_are_rows = TRUE), so the table is transposed. We also extract the metadata and the taxonomy.

[1] TRUE

tax_rare  <- data.frame(tax_table(otu_table_rarefy))[, c("phylum", "class",
                                                         "order", "family",

title: Indicator species
text:
Indicator species analysis
Indicator species analysis[1] tests, for each OTU, how strongly it is associated with a group of samples (here, a land use). indicspecies::multipatt() also tests combinations of groups: an OTU can be associated with several land uses together (e.g. both agricultural land uses), not only with one[2].
Two association indices are commonly used:

IndVal ("IndVal.g"): combines the specificity of the OTU (is it found mostly in this group?) and its fidelity (is it found in most samples of this group?). It only looks for OTUs that are associated with a group (preference).
Point-biserial correlation ("r.g"): the correlation between the abundance of the OTU and the membership to a group. It can also be negative (avoidance), and it considers the abundances outside the group.

As in the tutorial, we use "r.g". The .g versions correct for the different number of samples in each group, important here because the oak group has many more samples. The p-values are obtained by permutations: the samples are randomly assigned to the groups 999 times. This takes about 30 seconds.

set.seed(100)
indval <- multipatt(otu_mat, meta_rare$Land_use, func = "r.g",
                    control = how(nperm = 999))

The results are in indval$sign: for each OTU, the columns s.<group> show to which group(s) it is associated (1 = yes), index the number of the group combination, stat the value of the correlation and p.value the p-value of the permutation test.

Multiple testing
One test is done for each of the 5153 OTUs. With a threshold of 0.05, about 5% of the OTUs (~250) would be significant by chance only. The tutorial therefore uses a stricter threshold of p ≤ 0.001.

sum(indval$sign$p.value <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 895

sum(indval$sign$p.value <= 0.001, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 280


The p-values can also be corrected for multiple testing, e.g. with the false discovery rate (FDR) of Benjamini & Hochberg. With 999 permutations, the smallest possible p-value is 0.001: to obtain smaller corrected p-values, more permutations would be needed.

p_fdr <- p.adjust(indval$sign$p.value, method = "fdr")
sum(p_fdr <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 349


We keep the OTUs with p ≤ 0.001, as in the tutorial: 280 OTUs (tutorial: 287).

indval_sig <- subset(indval$sign, p.value <= 0.001)
nrow(indval_sig)

[1] 280

indval_tab <- cbind(indval_sig[, c("Land_uses", "stat", "p.value")],

indval_tab <- indval_tab[order(indval_sig$index, -indval_sig$stat), ]

The six plantations differ from each other (see Beta diversity), so few OTUs are found consistently in all of them. 20 OTUs are associated with both agricultural land uses together.


Taxonomy of the indicator OTUs
We count the indicator OTUs per land use (or combination) and phylum. The OTUs without a phylum are “Unidentified”, and the phyla with few indicator OTUs are grouped as “Other” (the colour palette has 8 colours).

indval_tab$phylum_plot <- ifelse(is.na(indval_tab$phylum) |
                                   indval_tab$phylum == "NA",
                                 "Unidentified", indval_tab$phylum)
top_phyla <- names(sort(table(indval_tab$phylum_plot), decreasing = TRUE))[1:7]
indval_tab$phylum_plot[!indval_tab$phylum_plot %in% top_phyla] <- "Other"

indval_phylum <- count(indval_tab, Land_uses, phylum = phylum_plot)

# Order the land use combinations by their index (single land uses at the
# top of the plot), and put "Other" and "Unidentified" at the end of the
# legend
indval_phylum$Land_uses <- factor(
  indval_phylum$Land_uses,
  levels = rev(unique(indval_tab$Land_uses)))
indval_phylum$phylum <- factor(
  indval_phylum$phylum,
  levels = c(sort(setdiff(top_phyla, c("Other", "Unidentified"))),
             "Other", "Unidentified"))

p_indval_phylum <- ggplot(indval_phylum,
                          aes(x = n, y = Land_uses, fill = phylum)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = "Number of indicator OTUs", y = NULL, fill = "Phylum") +
  theme_bw()
p_indval_phylum








Ascomycota are the most common indicators of the agricultural land uses and the grassland. Many indicators of the old forest belong to Rozellomycota (20 of 55 OTUs), a group of parasites of other fungi and protists, mostly known from environmental sequences.

We plot the abundance of the strongest indicator OTU of each single land use. The OTU names are long sequence identifiers, so the plot labels use the genus (or the lowest identified rank) instead. psmelt() converts the phyloseq object into a long data frame (one row per OTU and sample), convenient for ggplot.

  tibble::rownames_to_column("OTU") %>%
  filter(Land_uses %in% levels(meta_rare$Land_use)) %>%
  group_by(Land_uses) %>%
  slice_max(stat, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(factor(Land_uses, levels = levels(meta_rare$Land_use)))

The strongest indicators of the agricultural land uses and of the grassland are abundant in all samples of their land use and rare or absent elsewhere, e.g. the Mortierella OTU of organic agriculture (r = 0.97) has 7 to 18 reads in every organic agriculture sample, and almost none in the other land uses. The indicator of the oak plantations, a Penicillium OTU, has a weaker association (r = 0.65): it is absent from the open land uses, but its abundance varies a lot between the plantation samples, and it is also found in the old forest. The indicator of the old forest, a Solicoccozyma OTU, is present in all land uses but much more abundant in the old forest: the point-biserial correlation also detects differences in abundance, not only in presence.






Note



Indicator OTUs are useful to describe the groups, but the taxonomy of many of them is incomplete: e.g. the indicator of conventional agriculture is only identified to the family Plectosphaerellaceae.

title: Indicator species
text:
Regression models for multivariate abundances
Indicator species analysis uses permutation tests, which do not account for the strong mean-variance relationship of count data: abundant OTUs also vary much more between samples (overdispersion). An alternative is to fit a generalised linear model (GLM) to each OTU, with a distribution suited to overdispersed counts, such as the negative binomial. The mvabund package[3] fits these models with manyglm() and tests them with resampling (bootstrap).
Resampling is slow with many OTUs. To keep the computation time short, we only use the OTUs present in at least 10% of the samples (9 of 87): rare OTUs, present in a few samples, carry little information for a GLM anyway.

prev <- colSums(otu_mat > 0)
otu_mat_prev <- otu_mat[, prev >= 9]
ncol(otu_mat_prev)

[1] 402


We convert the matrix into an mvabund object, and fit a negative binomial GLM to each OTU, with the land use as explanatory variable.

otu_mvabund <- mvabund(otu_mat_prev)

glm_lu <- manyglm(otu_mvabund ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare,
                  family = "negative.binomial")

Check the model: the residuals should be spread randomly around 0, without a fan shape (which would mean that the negative binomial distribution does not describe the mean-variance relationship well).

plot(glm_lu)








The residuals are spread evenly around 0, without a fan shape: the negative binomial distribution is suitable. The vertical lines on the left are OTUs that are absent from all samples of a land use (very low predicted abundance); they are common with sparse data such as OTU tables.
We test the effect of the land use with anova(). nBoot is the number of bootstrap resamplings: we use 100 for a fast (about 1 minute) but less precise result. For a publication, use e.g. 999. p.uni = "adjusted" also tests each OTU separately, with p-values adjusted for multiple testing.

set.seed(100)
anova_lu <- anova(glm_lu, nBoot = 100, p.uni = "adjusted",
                  show.time = "none")


# Multivariate test: does the land use affect the community as a whole?
anova_lu$table

(Intercept)     86      NA       NA         NA
Land_use        82       4 11762.67 0.00990099


mvabund changes the OTU names that start with a number (it adds an “X”), so we take the names from our matrix instead (same order).

# Univariate tests: which OTUs differ between land uses?
p_uni <- anova_lu$uni.p["Land_use", ]
otus_glm_sig <- colnames(otu_mat_prev)[p_uni <= 0.05]
length(otus_glm_sig)

[1] 180


The land use has a significant effect on the community as a whole (p = 0.01, the smallest p-value possible with 100 resamplings: 1/101). 180 of the 402 OTUs differ significantly between land uses (adjusted p ≤ 0.05).

Coefficients
The coefficients of the significant OTUs (one column per OTU). The reference (intercept) is the first level of Land_use, conventional agriculture. A negative coefficient means that the OTU is less abundant in that land use than in conventional agriculture, a positive one that it is more abundant. We look at the 6 most abundant significant OTUs.

coefs <- coef(glm_lu)[, p_uni <= 0.05]
colnames(coefs) <- otus_glm_sig

title: Alpha diversity
text:
Alpha diversity describes the diversity within a single sample. It can be summarized by several measures, such as richness (the number of OTUs), Shannon diversity or Simpson diversity. These measures differ in how much weight they give to rare OTUs compared to abundant ones, and therefore capture different aspects of the community.
This section documents how to rarefy the data before calculating alpha diversity, how to check whether the sequencing depth is sufficient to capture the diversity of the samples using rarefaction and extrapolation curves, and how to compare richness between sites using either rarefied or estimated richness. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 010_alpha_diversity.R and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.
Download script


 


 Download example RData
To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see BLAST filtering). For reproducibility, set seeds (random number generation) at the start of the script to always obtain the same results with rarefaction.
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
set.seed(100)

title: Alpha diversity
text:
Rarefaction
Alpha diversity, and richness in particular, depends strongly on sequencing depth: samples with more reads inevitably contain more OTUs (see Rarefaction & Normalization). Before comparing alpha diversity between samples, the data must therefore be standardized. For alpha diversity, rarefaction is recommended[1], even when other standardization methods are used for beta diversity: all samples are randomly subsampled to the same number of reads.
How to choose the rarefaction depth, and how many reads and OTUs are lost by rarefying, is explained in Rarefaction & Normalization. In this example, we rarefy to 1011 reads: the two samples with fewer reads (120 and 487 reads) are removed.
phyloseq::rarefy_even_depth() subsamples all samples to the same depth:

sample.size: the rarefaction depth. Samples with fewer reads are removed.
replace = FALSE: subsampling without replacement (like drawing reads out of the sample one at a time).
rngseed: the seed for the random subsampling, for reproducibility.

OTUs that are no longer present in any sample after subsampling are removed automatically.

# Save the chosen rarefaction depth (you can change it, see Exercise 1)
rare_depth <- 1011

# Rarefy all samples to the chosen depth
otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, sample.size = rare_depth,
                                      replace = FALSE, rngseed = 100)

`set.seed(100)` was used to initialize repeatable random subsampling.

Rarefying discards about 75% of the reads, from the samples with a high sequencing depth. An alternative to rarefying is to extrapolate alpha diversity based on the accumulation of OTUs with increasing numbers of reads (see below).

title: Alpha diversity
text:
Interpolation and extrapolation with iNEXT
The R package iNEXT[2,3] draws rarefaction (interpolation) and extrapolation curves, and estimates the diversity each sample would have if it was sequenced completely (asymptotic diversity). phyloseq has no equivalent function for this, so we extract the OTU table from the phyloseq object and use iNEXT directly.






NoteHill numbers



iNEXT uses Hill numbers of order q[4,5]:

q = 0: species richness (number of OTUs)
q = 1: Shannon diversity (the exponential of the Shannon entropy)
q = 2: Simpson diversity (the inverse of the Simpson concentration)

Larger numbers always mean higher diversity. Hill numbers are expressed in “effective number of OTUs”: the number of equally abundant OTUs that would give the same diversity. As q increases, rare OTUs get less weight. Expressing all three measures in the same unit makes them directly comparable.



Run iNEXT for each sample
iNEXT expects a data frame with OTUs as rows and samples as columns. Use the non-rarefied data: iNEXT does its own rarefaction and extrapolation.

# Convert the OTU table to a data frame with OTUs as rows
otu_df <- as.data.frame(as(otu_table(otu_BLAST_clean), "matrix"))
if (!taxa_are_rows(otu_BLAST_clean)) otu_df <- as.data.frame(t(otu_df))

iNEXT() is run on each sample individually:

q: the orders of the Hill numbers to calculate.
datatype = "abundance": the data are read counts per OTU.
endpoint: the number of reads up to which the curves are drawn. Beyond the library size of a sample, the curve is extrapolated. Extrapolation is only reliable up to about twice the library size of the sample[2]. Here, we draw the curves up to 10000 reads, slightly more than the largest library size (8506 reads).
knots: the number of points calculated along each curve. Fewer knots make the calculation faster.







WarningiNEXT takes a long time to run



iNEXT calculates the curves and their confidence intervals (by bootstrapping) for each sample and each order q. For this dataset, it takes about 10 minutes, but it can take hours for larger or more deeply sequenced datasets. In that case, run it before a long break or overnight. Save the result so that you do not have to run it again, and load it next time instead.



# Run iNEXT for each sample individually (it takes about 10 minutes...)
inext_res <- iNEXT(otu_df, q = c(0, 1, 2), datatype = "abundance",
                   endpoint = 10000, knots = 20)

# Save the iNEXT results, and load them next time instead of running iNEXT
save(inext_res, file = "RData/ITS/inext_res.RData")
# load("RData/ITS/inext_res.RData")



Plot the curves
The rarefaction (solid lines) and extrapolation (dashed lines) curves of each sample are plotted with one panel per order q. The vertical line shows the rarefaction depth.

p_inext <- ggiNEXT(inext_res, type = 1, facet.var = "Order.q", grey = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_depth) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_inext








If the curves reach a plateau before the rarefaction depth (vertical line), the rarefied data capture the diversity of the samples for this order q. If the curves are still increasing at the rarefaction depth, more OTUs would be found with more sequencing, and the rarefied diversity underestimates the diversity of the samples.
Shannon and Simpson diversity (q = 1 and q = 2) give less weight to rare OTUs and level off around or before the rarefaction depth. Richness (q = 0), instead, is still rising steeply at 1011 reads. Richness is very sensitive to rare OTUs and to sequencing depth, and therefore requires the most caution: with the low rarefaction depth of this dataset, the rarefaction curves in Rarefaction & Normalization also showed that richness is far from a plateau.


Estimated (asymptotic) diversity
iNEXT returns a table with the observed and estimated (asymptotic) diversity of each sample, for each order q. For richness (q = 0), the estimator is the Chao1 estimator[6].

NoteWhy we kept singletons



Chao1 estimates the number of undetected OTUs from the number of OTUs that occur only once (singletons) or twice (doubletons) in a sample. This is why we did not remove singletons and rare OTUs during global filtering: removing them would remove the information the estimator relies on, and the estimated richness would be underestimated.

title: Alpha diversity
text:
Rarefied vs estimated richness
What is the impact of using the estimated species richness instead of the rarefied species richness?

Calculate richness
The rarefied richness is calculated with phyloseq::estimate_richness(), which calculates several alpha diversity measures at once. "Observed" is the number of OTUs in each sample. estimate_richness() returns the samples in the same order as the phyloseq object, with sample names as row names.

# Rarefied richness
SR <- estimate_richness(otu_table_rarefy, measures = "Observed") %>%
  dplyr::rename(SRrare = Observed)
SR$Assemblage <- rownames(SR)

# Estimated richness from iNEXT
SR_est <- inext_div %>%
  filter(Diversity == "Species richness") %>%
  select(Assemblage, Estimator)

# Combine the two tables, keeping only the samples present in both
SR <- inner_join(SR, SR_est, by = "Assemblage")

# Add the sample data (site and land use)
meta <- as(sample_data(otu_table_rarefy), "data.frame")
SR$SiteID <- meta[SR$Assemblage, "SiteID"]

Compare richness between sites

title: Rarefaction and other normalization methods
text:
The most commonly used methods to standardize sequencing depth across samples are rarefaction and data transformation. These two strategies are currently at the center of an ongoing debate in the field, as they rely on fundamentally different statistical assumptions about amplicon data. Rarefaction equalizes library sizes by subsampling reads to a common depth and has long been used in ecology, but it discards data and reduces statistical power, leading some to argue that it is statistically inadmissible[1]. Proponents of compositional data analysis emphasize that sequencing data are inherently compositional and should be analyzed using log-ratio transformations (e.g., CLR) and Aitchison geometry, rather than through subsampling (rarefaction) or count-based normalization (relative abundance)[2]. However, rarefaction has recently been defended as a pragmatic and robust approach for controlling uneven sequencing effort in diversity analyses, emphasizing its interpretability and long-standing use in ecology[3]. Ultimately, the debate centers on a fundamental statistical question: whether sequencing counts should be treated as compositional data requiring ratio-based transformations, or as sampling-based counts for which subsampling remains an acceptable ecological standardization strategy.
To our knowledge, rarefying can more effectively mitigate the artifact of sample library size than other normalization techniques, especially for small (<1000 sequences per sample) and very uneven (>~10× on average) library sizes[4]. Other normalization approaches are prone to generation of artifactual clusters based on sequencing depth in beta diversity analysis, and higher false discovery rates in differential abundance testing. When sequencing depth is sufficient and balanced, other compositional methods are generally better suited because they preserve statistical power[1]. For alpha diversity comparisons, rarefaction is always recommended[3]. In any case, researchers should proceed with caution and check for library size effects if the count data was not rarefied, as demonstrated below (see Check for library size effects).
This section documents how to explore the sequencing depth of your samples, how to rarefy the data, how to apply other standardization methods, and how to compare them. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 006_normalization.R and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.
Download script


 


 Download example RData
To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see BLAST filtering). For reproducibility, set seeds (random number generation) at the start of the script to always obtain the same results with rarefaction.
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
set.seed(42)

title: Rarefaction and other normalization methods
text:
Rarefaction
Rarefaction normalizes sequencing depth by randomly subsampling reads so that all samples have the same library size, thereby facilitating direct comparison of diversity metrics across samples. While this approach improves comparability, it inevitably discards valid observations and can lead to substantial data loss depending on the chosen rarefaction threshold.
Before rarefying, we explore how the number of OTUs depends on the number of samples and on the number of reads. Several vegan functions used below expect a samples x taxa matrix, so we first extract the OTU table from the phyloseq object.

# Transpose the OTU table if taxa_are_rows is TRUE
otu_mat <- as(otu_table(otu_BLAST_clean), "matrix")
if (taxa_are_rows(otu_BLAST_clean)) otu_mat <- t(otu_mat)


Species accumulation curves
Most OTUs are rare and found in only a few samples (see Global filtering). This suggests that adding new samples to the study may lead to the continuous discovery of new OTUs. Species accumulation curves show how the total number of OTUs increases with the number of samples.
The function vegan::specaccum() calculates the accumulation curve of a group of samples. With method = "random", samples are added in a random order, and the curve is averaged over a number of random orders (permutations). Here, we calculate one curve per site.

# Identify the sites
sites <- unique(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$SiteID)

# Create an empty list to store the results of each site
accum_list <- list()

for (site in sites) {
  # Keep only the samples of the current site, and the OTUs present in them
  otu_site <- prune_samples(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$SiteID == site,
                            otu_BLAST_clean)
  otu_site <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_site) > 0, otu_site)

  # Convert to a samples x taxa matrix
  mat_site <- as(otu_table(otu_site), "matrix")
  if (taxa_are_rows(otu_site)) mat_site <- t(mat_site)

  # Run specaccum for this site
  sp <- specaccum(mat_site, method = "random", permutations = 100)

  # Save the results in a data frame
  accum_list[[site]] <- data.frame(Samples = sp$sites,
                                   Richness = sp$richness,
                                   SD = sp$sd,
                                   SiteID = site)
}

# Bind the data frames of all sites together
accum_data <- do.call(rbind, accum_list)

# Plot the accumulation curves (the ribbons show the standard deviation)
ggplot(accum_data, aes(x = Samples, y = Richness,
                       color = SiteID, fill = SiteID)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Richness - SD, ymax = Richness + SD),
              alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:max(accum_data$Samples)) +
  labs(x = "Number of samples", y = "Accumulated number of OTUs",
       title = "Species accumulation curves per site") +
  theme_classic()








The number of OTUs keeps increasing with the number of samples, and the curves do not reach a plateau: the fungal communities of the sites are not completely sampled. This is common in soil fungal data sets, which contain a very large number of rare OTUs.


Rarefaction curves
To assess whether the data are suitable for rarefaction, we can draw rarefaction curves. These curves plot the expected number of observed taxa as a function of sequencing depth for each sample, allowing us to evaluate whether diversity approaches a plateau. If most curves level off near the chosen threshold, sequencing depth is likely sufficient; if they continue to rise steeply, rarefaction at that depth may lead to substantial information loss.
The function vegan::rarecurve() calculates the curves. With tidy = TRUE, it returns a data frame instead of drawing a plot, so that we can plot it with ggplot2. The columns are Site (the sample name), Sample (the number of reads) and Species (the number of OTUs). The argument step gives the interval (in number of reads) between the points of the curves.

rare_curves <- rarecurve(otu_mat, step = 100, tidy = TRUE)

# Add the land use of each sample
meta_rare <- as(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean), "data.frame")
rare_curves$Land_use <- meta_rare[as.character(rare_curves$Site), "Land_use"]

# Plot the rarefaction curves, one panel per land use. The vertical line shows
# the rarefaction depth that we will choose below (1011 reads).
ggplot(rare_curves, aes(x = Sample, y = Species,
                        group = Site, color = Land_use)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1011, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ Land_use) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth (number of reads)",
       y = "Observed number of OTUs (richness)",
       color = "Land use",
       title = "Rarefaction curves") +
  theme_classic()








Each line is a sample. The samples have very different sequencing depths (from 120 to 8,506 reads), and the majority of the samples are far from reaching a plateau: the more reads in a sample, the more OTUs are discovered. Let’s check if this is the case.


Sequencing depth and richness
Do samples with a higher sequencing depth also have a larger number of OTUs?

# Number of OTUs per sample (richness)
seq_rich <- estimate_richness(otu_BLAST_clean, measures = "Observed")

# Add the number of reads per sample (sequencing depth)
seq_rich$reads <- sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)

min(seq_rich$Observed)  # sample with the lowest number of OTUs (36)
max(seq_rich$Observed)  # sample with the highest number of OTUs (738)
mean(seq_rich$Observed) # mean number of OTUs per sample (381)


# R2 of the linear regression between number of reads and number of OTUs
r2_depth <- summary(lm(Observed ~ reads, data = seq_rich))$r.squared

ggplot(seq_rich, aes(x = reads, y = Observed)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Number of reads in the sample", y = "Number of OTUs",
       subtitle = paste("R2 =", round(r2_depth, 3))) +
  theme_bw()








In microbiome data, the number of reads and the number of OTUs are generally correlated: samples with more reads inevitably contain more OTUs. In this example, the number of reads explains ~50% of the variation in the number of OTUs (R2 = 0.48). Ignoring this introduces a bias in alpha diversity estimates. This is why it is important to standardize the data!


Choose the rarefaction depth
Sequencing runs usually have uneven sequencing depths, with some samples having a low number of reads. Choosing a rarefaction depth determines which samples will be excluded from the analysis: all samples with fewer reads than the chosen depth are removed.

# Histogram of the sequencing depths
depth_df <- data.frame(depth = sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean))

ggplot(depth_df, aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Sequencing depth (number of reads)", y = "Number of samples") +
  theme_minimal()









# Check the number of reads of each sample, from smallest to largest
sort(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean))

# What is the smallest library size across samples? Is it sufficient?
min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)) # 120 reads

# Identify the next lowest library sizes
min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)[sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean) > 120]) # 487 reads
min(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)[sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean) > 487]) # 1011 reads

The two samples with the smallest library sizes (120 and 487 reads) are the low-depth samples identified in Dealing with negative controls. Rarefying all samples to 120 reads would discard almost all the information of the other samples. The next lowest library size is 1011 reads: if we choose this depth, we lose these two samples, but keep a reasonable number of reads in all others.
Rarefaction depth selection is inherently a trade-off between retaining samples and retaining reads per sample, and no published study provides a universally valid cutoff for the acceptable proportion of discarded samples. If several samples had a small library size, you could choose to rarefy to the size of the second, third, etc. lowest library size, until you find a sufficient depth.


Rarefy
The function phyloseq::rarefy_even_depth() subsamples all samples to the same depth (sample.size). Samples with fewer reads are removed. Without the argument sample.size, the function rarefies to the library size of the sample with the lowest library size.

# Choose the rarefaction depth (you can change it)
chosen_depth <- 1011

# Rarefy all samples to the chosen depth. Samples with fewer reads are removed.
otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, replace = F,
                                      sample.size = chosen_depth)

# Check the number of reads per sample: all samples should have the same depth
sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy)

# How many OTUs remained after rarefaction? OTUs that are no longer present in
# any sample are removed automatically by rarefy_even_depth().
ntaxa(otu_BLAST_clean)  # 9036 OTUs
ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy) # 5116 OTUs

# Was any sample discarded?
nsamples(otu_BLAST_clean) - nsamples(otu_table_rarefy) # 2 samples

# How many reads remain in the dataset, and what percentage of the reads is it?
sum(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy)) # 87957 reads
sum(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy)) / sum(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)) * 100 # 24.4%

After rarefaction, 87 samples and 5116 OTUs remain (out of 9036). Rarefying leads to the loss of many reads (here, ~75% of the reads), because it discards data from the samples with a high sequencing depth.






Note



Rarefaction is random: running it with a different seed gives slightly different results (e.g., a few OTUs more or less). For alpha diversity, an alternative to rarefying is to extrapolate diversity based on the accumulation of OTUs with increasing numbers of reads (see Alpha diversity). For other analyses, the transformations below do not discard any reads.




Are library sizes balanced between groups?
Finally, to check whether rarefaction is needed, we can compare library sizes between groups.

# Extract sample metadata
meta <- as(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean), "data.frame")

# Add library size
meta$library_size <- sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)

# Plot results
ggplot(meta, aes(x = SiteID, y = library_size)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_bw()








Simple statistical tests can support what we see in the boxplot.

# Test for homogeneity of variances
bartlett.test(library_size ~ SiteID, data = meta)


    Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances

data:  library_size by SiteID
Bartlett's K-squared = 23.297, df = 9, p-value = 0.005562

# Test for differences between groups
kruskal.test(library_size ~ SiteID, data = meta)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  library_size by SiteID
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 23.308, df = 9, p-value = 0.00554


These results show that the library sizes differ between sites, both in their variance (Bartlett test) and in their median (Kruskal-Wallis test): e.g., the samples of Oak_44 and Oak_54 have more reads than those of the agricultural sites. Because the number of OTUs depends on the number of reads, differences in library size between sites could be mistaken for differences in diversity. In this case, it is important to either rarefy the data, or to check that the results do not depend on library size (see Check for library size effects).
If the library sizes were balanced between groups (homogeneity of variance and equal medians) and sufficient in all samples (>1000 reads per sample), other compositional methods for normalization would be better suited than rarefaction, as they do not discard any reads.

title: Rarefaction and other normalization methods
text:
Transformations
The advantage of other standardization methods over rarefaction is to not discard any reads. Rather than removing information, these methods transform the counts of each sample so that samples become comparable. They are more and more commonly used instead of rarefaction.

Relative abundance transformations

Simple relative abundance
A simple transformation is the relative abundance: the counts of each sample are divided by the total number of reads of the sample. This method is presented here for demonstration purposes, but is not recommended in practice.

otu_table_rel <- transform_sample_counts(
  otu_BLAST_clean, function(x) x / sum(x))



Hellinger transformation
The Hellinger transformation converts species abundances from absolute to relative values (i.e., standardizes the abundances to sample totals) and then square roots them. It is recommended to use this transformation with count data to account for the arch effect regularly observed in ecological count data, and to make Euclidean-based methods (PCA, RDA) suitable for data with many zeros[5]. This transformation can be applied on both raw or rarefied data.

otu_table_hel <- transform_sample_counts(
  otu_BLAST_clean, function(x) sqrt(x / sum(x)))




Log-ratio transformations
Rarefaction and the Hellinger transformation preserve abundance data, which is constrained by the sample total (the compositional “closure” problem). On the other hand, ratios are invariant to total counts and therefore capture the scale-independent relationships among taxa. Log-ratio transformations thus have the advantage of solving compositionality, an important issue when doing ordinations[2].
Because these transformations assume strictly positive data (log(0) is undefined), zero imputation is required.






Warning



Zero replacement changes the data structure and can influence downstream inference, especially when zeros are structural (the taxon is truly absent) rather than below the detection limit.



CLR (centered log-ratio)
The CLR transformation reduces data skewness and compositionality bias. Each count is log-transformed, and the mean of the log-counts of the sample is subtracted. Here, the zeros are imputed by adding a pseudocount of 1 to all counts (x + 1). Note that the choice of pseudocount affects the result, especially for rare taxa.

otu_table_clr <- transform_sample_counts(otu_BLAST_clean, function(x) {
  lx <- log(x + 1)
  lx - mean(lx)
})



RCLR (robust CLR)
The RCLR transformation is similar to the CLR, but only uses the non-zero values of each sample, so that it allows data that contain zeros. However, this transformation is not a per-sample operation and cannot be performed using phyloseq::transform_sample_counts(). We use vegan::decostand() instead (see ?decostand for more information).

# Save OTU table using a new name
otu_table_rclr <- otu_BLAST_clean

# Extract OTU table from phyloseq object and convert to a matrix
mat <- as(otu_table(otu_table_rclr), "matrix")

# If taxa are rows in OTU table, the matrix must be transposed to be used
# with vegan::decostand (remember to transpose the matrix again before
# putting it back in the phyloseq object)
taxa_rows <- taxa_are_rows(otu_table_rclr)
if (taxa_rows) mat <- t(mat) # samples = rows for vegan

# rclr transformation
mat_rclr <- decostand(mat, "rclr", impute = TRUE)

# Put back row and column names (decostand removed them)
row.names(mat_rclr) <- row.names(mat)
colnames(mat_rclr) <- colnames(mat)

# Transpose again and put it back into phyloseq object
if (taxa_rows) mat_rclr <- t(mat_rclr) # taxa = rows for phyloseq
otu_table(otu_table_rclr) <- otu_table(mat_rclr, taxa_are_rows = taxa_rows)

title: Rarefaction and other normalization methods
text:
Compare the methods
Each standardization method changes the data in a different way. To see what this means in practice, we can compare ordinations of the same samples calculated with each method. If the main patterns (e.g., the separation of the sites) are similar across methods, our conclusions do not depend on the choice of standardization. If they differ, we need to understand why before moving on to statistical analyses.
A transformation and a distance measure always go together. Some combinations are standard because the distance is suited to the values produced by the transformation:

Table 1. Common combinations of standardization methods and distance measures







Standardization
Distance
Name of the combination




Rarefied counts
Bray-Curtis
Bray-Curtis


Relative abundance
Bray-Curtis
Bray-Curtis


Hellinger
Euclidean
Hellinger distance


CLR
Euclidean
Aitchison distance


RCLR
Euclidean
Robust Aitchison distance



The Euclidean distance calculated on Hellinger-transformed data is called the Hellinger distance. This is the combination proposed by Legendre & Gallagher[5], and the one implied when running a PCA or RDA on Hellinger-transformed data. The Bray-Curtis distance can also be calculated on Hellinger-transformed data, and you will find this combination in the literature, but it is less straightforward to interpret. The Bray-Curtis distance cannot be used on CLR or RCLR data, because these contain negative values.
Below, we compare four of these combinations: rarefied counts, relative abundance, Hellinger and RCLR.

Use the same samples for all methods
The rarefied data no longer contain the two samples with a low library size, whereas the transformed data still contain them. To compare the methods, all OTU tables must contain the same samples: we remove these two samples from the transformed data too.

keep_samples <- sample_names(otu_table_rarefy)

otu_table_rel  <- prune_samples(keep_samples, otu_table_rel)
otu_table_hel  <- prune_samples(keep_samples, otu_table_hel)
otu_table_rclr <- prune_samples(keep_samples, otu_table_rclr)

The transformations are calculated for each sample separately, so removing samples afterwards does not change the values of the other samples. The only exception is the zero imputation of the RCLR transformation, which uses the whole table; the effect of the two removed samples is negligible.


Calculate the distance matrices
The function phyloseq::distance() calculates a distance matrix between samples from a phyloseq object. It uses vegan::vegdist() for most distance measures. We will use the distance matrices to compare the methods directly (see Compare the distance matrices).

# 1. Rarefied counts + Bray-Curtis
dist_rare <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rarefy, method = "bray")

# 2. Relative abundance + Bray-Curtis
dist_rel <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rel, method = "bray")

# 3. Hellinger + Euclidean (= Hellinger distance)
dist_hel <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_hel, method = "euclidean")

# 4. RCLR + Euclidean (= robust Aitchison distance)
dist_rclr <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rclr, method = "euclidean")







Note



vegan::vegdist() can also calculate the Aitchison and robust Aitchison distances directly from the raw counts, without transforming the data first, e.g., vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison"). This gives a different result from the code above, because the zeros are handled differently: we imputed them with decostand() when creating otu_table_rclr (impute = TRUE), whereas vegdist() does not impute them. Be consistent and report which approach you used.




NMDS ordinations
NMDS (non-metric multidimensional scaling) represents the distances between samples in a small number of dimensions (here, k = 2). NMDS only uses the rank order of the distances, which makes it suitable for any distance measure.
The function phyloseq::ordinate() calculates the distance matrix and runs the NMDS (vegan::metaMDS()) in one step. The distance measure is given by its name, e.g., distance = "bray". Additional arguments are passed on to metaMDS():

k: number of dimensions of the ordination;
trymax: maximum number of random starts used to find the best solution. NMDS is an iterative method that starts from random configurations. The seed set at the start of the script makes the results reproducible, as long as the script is run from the start;
autotransform = FALSE: by default, metaMDS() applies a square root and a Wisconsin double standardization to count data. We turn this off, so that each ordination is calculated on the data as we transformed them above;
trace = FALSE: hides the progress messages.







Warning



ordinate() also accepts a distance matrix that was already calculated (e.g., distance = dist_rare), but in that case it ignores all additional arguments and silently uses the default settings of metaMDS().



nmds_rare <- ordinate(otu_table_rarefy, method = "NMDS", distance = "bray",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)
nmds_rel  <- ordinate(otu_table_rel, method = "NMDS", distance = "bray",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)
nmds_hel  <- ordinate(otu_table_hel, method = "NMDS", distance = "euclidean",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)
nmds_rclr <- ordinate(otu_table_rclr, method = "NMDS", distance = "euclidean",
                      k = 2, trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE)

'comm' has negative data: 'autotransform', 'noshare' and 'wascores' set to FALSE


Printing an NMDS object shows the stress and whether a convergent solution was found. If it says “Best solution was not repeated”, increase trymax before interpreting the ordination.

nmds_rare


Call:
metaMDS(comm = veganifyOTU(physeq), distance = distance, k = 2,      trymax = 100, autotransform = FALSE, trace = FALSE) 

global Multidimensional Scaling using monoMDS

Data:     veganifyOTU(physeq) 
Distance: bray 

Dimensions: 2 
Stress:     0.1846445 
Stress type 1, weak ties
Best solution was repeated 1 time in 30 tries
The best solution was from try 14 (random start)
Scaling: centring, PC rotation, halfchange scaling 
Species: expanded scores based on 'veganifyOTU(physeq)' 


The stress value indicates how well the 2D ordination represents the original distances. As a rule of thumb, stress < 0.1 is good, 0.1-0.2 is acceptable, and > 0.2 should be interpreted with caution.

nmds_stress <- c(Rarefied  = nmds_rare$stress,
                 RelAbund  = nmds_rel$stress,
                 Hellinger = nmds_hel$stress,
                 RCLR      = nmds_rclr$stress)
round(nmds_stress, 3)

 Rarefied  RelAbund Hellinger      RCLR 
    0.185     0.179     0.169     0.050 


To compare the ordinations, we plot them side by side, with the samples coloured by site. The stress value is added to each plot.

plot_nmds <- function(physeq, ord, title) {
  plot_ordination(physeq, ord, color = "SiteID") +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = paste("Stress =", round(ord$stress, 3))) +
    theme_bw()
}

p_rare <- plot_nmds(otu_table_rarefy, nmds_rare, "Rarefied + Bray-Curtis")

Warning: `aes_string()` was deprecated in ggplot2 3.0.0.
ℹ Please use tidy evaluation idioms with `aes()`.
ℹ See also `vignette("ggplot2-in-packages")` for more information.
ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the phyloseq package.
  Please report the issue at <https://github.com/joey711/phyloseq/issues>.

p_rel  <- plot_nmds(otu_table_rel,    nmds_rel,  "Relative abundance + Bray-Curtis")
p_hel  <- plot_nmds(otu_table_hel,    nmds_hel,  "Hellinger + Euclidean")
p_rclr <- plot_nmds(otu_table_rclr,   nmds_rclr, "RCLR + Euclidean (robust Aitchison)")

ggarrange(p_rare, p_rel, p_hel, p_rclr,
          ncol = 2, nrow = 2, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "right")








When comparing the plots, keep in mind that the orientation of NMDS axes is arbitrary: an ordination can be rotated or mirrored without changing its meaning. Focus on which samples group together and which groups are separated, not on the position of the groups in the plot.


Compare the distance matrices
The plots give a visual impression, but we can also measure how similar the methods are. The Mantel test calculates the correlation between two distance matrices. A correlation close to 1 means that both methods rank the distances between samples in the same way.

dist_list <- list(Rarefied  = dist_rare,
                  RelAbund  = dist_rel,
                  Hellinger = dist_hel,
                  RCLR      = dist_rclr)

# Create an empty matrix to store the Mantel correlations
mantel_r <- matrix(NA, nrow = length(dist_list), ncol = length(dist_list),
                   dimnames = list(names(dist_list), names(dist_list)))

# Calculate the Mantel correlation (Spearman) for each pair of methods
for (i in names(dist_list)) {
  for (j in names(dist_list)) {
    mantel_r[i, j] <- mantel(dist_list[[i]], dist_list[[j]],
                             method = "spearman", permutations = 0)$statistic
  }
}
round(mantel_r, 2)

          Rarefied RelAbund Hellinger RCLR
Rarefied      1.00     0.99      0.97 0.62
RelAbund      0.99     1.00      0.97 0.64
Hellinger     0.97     0.97      1.00 0.64
RCLR          0.62     0.64      0.64 1.00


Here, permutations = 0 skips the permutation test, because we are only interested in the correlation. Distances between the same samples are not independent, so we would not interpret a p-value in this context.
Rarefaction and relative abundance usually give very similar results, as both are based on proportions. The RCLR transformation is usually the most different, because it gives more weight to rare taxa, whereas Bray-Curtis is dominated by the most abundant taxa.
In this example, the rarefied, relative abundance and Hellinger distances are almost identical (r ≥ 0.97), and the four NMDS plots show a similar overall pattern: the agricultural sites and the grassland separate from the oak forests. The RCLR distances are less correlated with the others (r ~ 0.6): with RCLR, the grassland separates more strongly from the agricultural sites, whereas the old oak forest (Oak_ref) is less distinct from the other oak forests. Note also the much lower stress of the RCLR ordination.


Check for library size effects
If the data are not rarefied, differences in library size between samples can still affect the results. A simple way to check for this is to test whether library size explains a part of the variation in the ordinations.
The function vegan::envfit() fits a variable onto an ordination and tests how much of the variation in sample positions it explains (r2). We use the original library sizes (before rarefaction) for all methods, so that we can check whether each method has removed the effect of sequencing depth. Library sizes are log-transformed because they vary over an order of magnitude.

# Original library sizes of the samples used in the ordinations, in the same
# sample order as the ordinations
log_lib <- data.frame(
  log_library_size = log10(sample_sums(otu_BLAST_clean)[keep_samples]))

ord_list <- list(Rarefied  = nmds_rare,
                 RelAbund  = nmds_rel,
                 Hellinger = nmds_hel,
                 RCLR      = nmds_rclr)

# Fit library size onto each ordination and store the r2 and p-values
lib_fit <- t(sapply(ord_list, function(ord) {
  fit <- envfit(ord, log_lib, permutations = 999)
  c(r2 = unname(fit$vectors$r), p = unname(fit$vectors$pvals))
}))
round(lib_fit, 3)

             r2     p
Rarefied  0.069 0.069
RelAbund  0.074 0.032
Hellinger 0.108 0.009
RCLR      0.096 0.016


A low r2 and a non-significant p-value mean that library size does not explain the position of the samples in the ordination. If library size has a strong effect with the transformations, but not with rarefaction, consider using rarefied data. Note that if library size differs between groups (which we tested above), its effect cannot be separated from the effect of the groups.
In this example, library size has no significant effect on the rarefied ordination (p > 0.05), but it explains a small and significant part of the variation in the relative abundance, Hellinger and RCLR ordinations (p < 0.05). A likely reason is that deeper sequenced samples detect more rare taxa (fewer zeros), which affects the transformations that do not discard reads. However, we saw above that library sizes also differ between sites: part of this effect may be due to the sites themselves.
For a visual check, the ordinations can also be coloured by library size:

sample_data(otu_table_rclr)$log_library_size <- log_lib$log_library_size

plot_ordination(otu_table_rclr, nmds_rclr, color = "log_library_size") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "RCLR + Euclidean, coloured by library size") +
  theme_bw()

title: Rarefaction and other normalization methods
text:
Which method to choose?
This demonstration shows why it is important to check for library size effects when the data are not rarefied. With the low and uneven sequencing depth of this ITS data set, and library sizes that differ between sites, rarefied data are a safe choice. In this workflow:

Alpha diversity is compared on data rarefied to 1011 reads, and with rarefaction/extrapolation curves (iNEXT), which use all reads;
Beta diversity and the following analyses compare several transformations (e.g., Hellinger on rarefied data, and CLR for the Aitchison distance).

Each of these scripts starts again from otu_BLAST_clean.RData and applies the standardization it needs, using the code shown on this page.






Important



Whichever method you choose, report it (including the rarefaction depth or the pseudocount), and check that your conclusions do not depend on it.

title: BLAST quality check
text:
Filtering based on BLAST accuracy is applied to remove OTUs with low-confidence taxonomic assignments, typically indicated by low sequence similarity (pident), poor alignment coverage (qcovs), or poor fit of the rank resolution (evalue)[1]. Such features are frequently artefactual or biologically uninterpretable and can bias ecological inference if retained.
This section documents how to filter OTUs based on BLAST results (see table above), and clean the taxonomy assignations based on BLAST accuracy, in phyloseq objects. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 005_BLAST_filter.R and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, some studies also suggest to filter out sequences with less than 15% query coverage (qcovs), which are assumed to be fully synthetic[6]. In these cases, even though the query sequence may be long, if it has such a low alignment with the sequences in the database, it cannot be considered natural.
Note that the threshold at a query cover of 15% was determined arbitrarily. The authors denote: “This was guided by not wanting to pick too high a level, lest we exclude natural sequences […]. Similarly, we did not want to pick too low a level, since BLASTn searches preferentially for highly identical regions, and thus might cut off the end of a synthetic sequence yielding a maximal-scoring segment pair with lower query coverage and higher percentage identity (thus falsely classified as natural)”[6].
This demonstration is done with the ITS data, and we choose to remove sequences with a length (qlen) shorter than 100 bp or a query cover (qcovs) smaller than 15%.






Tipremove_taxa



Homemade function remove_taxa (loaded with 001_required_packages.R): a simplified way of removing a selection of OTU from a phyloseq object.

remove_taxa <- function(badTaxa, physeq){
  allTaxa <- taxa_names(physeq)
  cleanTaxa <- allTaxa[!(allTaxa %in% badTaxa)]
  return(prune_taxa(cleanTaxa, physeq))
}




# Extract BLAST results from OTU table
BLAST_rare <- as.data.frame(otu_table_rare@tax_table) %>%

title: BLAST quality check
text:
BLAST cleaning
After filtering out any remaining potential artefacts, BLAST statistics (such as pident and evalue) can also be used to confirm taxonomic assignations. At this stage, OTUs are not removed, as they are not considered artefacts anymore, but simply unknown species. This means that, based on specific thresholds for each target gene and taxonomic rank (Table 3), any taxonomic assignation below these thresholds is replaced with NA.

Unknown organisms
There are a few exceptions to this rule. As a rule of thumb (arbitrary thresholds):

Any OTU with an identity (pident) below 70% cannot be identified, even up to the kingdom level[7].
Any OTU with an e-value (evalue) above e-20 cannot be identified, even up to the kingdom level[7].
Any OTU with a query coverage (qcovs) below 50% must be investigated[6].
OTUs with an e-value between e-20 and e-50 should be manually checked against the 10 best BLAST matches for accurate assignment[7].

These OTUs should be further investigated to determine if they should be removed or preserved.

# Identify unknown OTUs
BLAST_unknown <- filter(BLAST_filter, pident < 70 | evalue > 1e-50 | qcovs < 50)
nrow(BLAST_unknown) # 1078 OTUs

# How many reads do they represent?
sum(taxa_sums(otu_BLAST_filter)[BLAST_unknown$taxa_OTU]) # 5474 reads (~1.5%)


# Look at the unknown OTUs
View(BLAST_unknown)







To which phyla were these OTUs assigned?

# Number of unknown OTUs per phylum ("." = no assignation)

In a smaller data set, these OTUs could be investigated one by one: a manual check against the 10 best BLAST matches allows for an accurate assignment. To do so, make sure to use the same database as the one used to generate your OTU table in the first place. For example, the OTU tables for each target gene were generated using the following databases:

SILVA for Bacteria and Archaea (16S)
UNITE for the eukaryotic nuclear ribosomal ITS region
BOLD identification engine for animal identification (CO1)

OTUs that cannot be confidently identified as Fungi could then be removed.






Tip



Create a FASTA file
To manually BLAST all sequences at once, create a FASTA file from your sequences and OTU ID, using the R package Biostrings.

# Extract sequences
fasta_seqs <- DNAStringSet(BLAST_unknown$query_seq)

# Name sequences with OTU ID
names(fasta_seqs) <- BLAST_unknown$taxa_OTU

# Write FASTA file
writeXStringSet(fasta_seqs, "BLAST_unknown.fasta")



Here, more than 1000 OTUs fall in this category, which makes a manual check impractical. Many of them belong to groups of fungi that are poorly represented in reference databases, such as Rozellomycota and Zoopagomycota, which explains why their BLAST matches are weak. Together, they represent only ~1.5% of the reads. We therefore keep these OTUs, but we do not trust their taxonomy below the kingdom level: their assignation at all ranks below kingdom will be removed (see below).

# Identify OTUs that should only be assigned to the kingdom level
otu_BLAST_assign <- BLAST_unknown[["taxa_OTU"]]

Before keeping them, let’s check that these OTUs do not dominate any sample, by visualizing the proportion of their reads in each sample:

# Proportion of reads belonging to these OTUs in each sample
unknown_prop <- data.frame(
  sample_data(otu_BLAST_filter),
  prop_unknown = sample_sums(prune_taxa(otu_BLAST_assign, otu_BLAST_filter)) /
    sample_sums(otu_BLAST_filter) * 100)

  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, size = 1) +
  labs(x = "Site", y = "Reads of OTUs with uncertain BLAST matches (%)") +
  theme_bw()








In all samples, these OTUs represent a small proportion of the reads, thus keeping them will not affect community analyses.


Rank-level confidence
Now that we are confident about our OTU selection, it is time to clean the taxonomy assignation. BLASTn searches preferentially for highly identical regions, and thus might cut off the ends of a synthetic sequence (not a real ITS fragment) yielding a maximal-scoring segment pair with lower query coverage and higher percentage identity, thus falsely classifying it as a real ITS match. Therefore, we must verify the pident to decide if we can trust the BLAST results. The table below summarizes thresholds for each target gene and taxonomic rank found in the literature.
