Based on the thresholds identified in Table 3, any taxonomic assignation below these thresholds will be changed to NA. For example, for an OTU identified to the species level, but that only has a pident of 95%, there is no certainty on the taxonomic assignation up to that rank. However, a pident of 95% allows for certainty up to the genus level. Thus, for this OTU, we would simply remove the assignation at the species level (replace it with NA) and preserve the other ranks.
For ITS, we use the rules of thumb of Tedersoo et al. (“ITS (rot)” in Table 3): species 98%, genus 90%, family 85%, order 80%, class 75% and phylum 75%[7,8,14]. In the ITS reference database, ranks without assignation are written as .: we first replace them with NA, so that all missing assignations are written the same way.

# Clean the OTU table based on taxonomy thresholds
# (remove assignation if confidence is too low).
BLAST_clean <- BLAST_filter %>%
  # Replace missing assignations (".") with "NA"
  mutate(across(phylum:species, ~ if_else(.x == ".", "NA", .x))) %>%
  mutate(species = if_else(pident < 98, "NA", species),
         genus = if_else(pident < 90, "NA", genus),
         family = if_else(pident < 85, "NA", family),
         order = if_else(pident < 80, "NA", order),
         class = if_else(pident < 75, "NA", class),
         phylum = if_else(pident < 75, "NA", phylum)) %>%
  # Remove uncultured assignation
  mutate(across(phylum:species, ~ gsub(".*uncultured.*", "NA", .x))) %>%
  # Remove metagenome assignation
  mutate(across(phylum:species, ~ gsub(".*metagenome.*", "NA", .x))) %>%
  # Remove assignation below kingdom for previously identified OTUs
  mutate(across(phylum:species, ~ if_else(taxa_OTU %in% otu_BLAST_assign, "NA", .x)))

The cleaned taxonomy table (BLAST_clean) should now be put back into the OTU table (phyloseq object).

title: Dealing with controls
text:
During DNA extraction, library preparation and sequencing, technical blanks, negative controls and positive controls may be added to detect contamination, confirm successful amplification of target genes, detect false results, and overall, verify that the full workflow (from extraction to bioinformatics) behaves as expected[1]. Field blanks (e.g., empty tubes left opened at the site or extraction of sample storage buffer) may also be included to enable removal of site or sampling material contaminants a posteriori[2].
This section documents how we analyse control samples and translate those results into practical actions in the data set. Using the R package decontam, the workflow enables identification and removal of contaminant DNA sequences based on patterns observed in blanks and negative controls[3]. In addition, positive controls can be used to evaluate whether the observed community composition matches the expected taxonomic profile[2].
The two downloadable scripts below (003_positive_control.R and 003_negative_control.R) implement a standard approach for dealing with negative and positive controls in a phyloseq object.



 


 Download script 003_positive_control


 


 Download script 003_negative_control


 



For a step-by-step explanation of how each control type is handled, explore the two sections below:

Dealing with positive controls
Dealing with negative controls (and blanks)

title: Dealing with negative controls
text:
This section documents how to inspect negative controls (or blanks) and remove contaminant DNA sequences using the R package decontam[1].
To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 003_negative_control.R and the example raw data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.



 


 Download script


 


 Download example RData


 




Inspect samples
Before using the package decontam to remove contaminants, we must first inspect samples (and controls) to determine if there are any visible problems. We can do this by comparing library size between samples, visualizing the prevalence of OTUs in samples and controls and visualizing the relative abundance of potential contaminants in all samples.

# Load OTU table
load("RData/ITS/otu_table_raw.RData")


Library size
The library size (a.k.a. the sequencing depth) of each sample can be predicted based on the type of samples you work with. For example, with soil samples, we expect abundant microbial communities, with hundreds if not thousands of sequences per sample. On the other hand, negative controls and blanks should have very small library sizes.

# Summarize sequencing depth per sample
seq_depth <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_raw)) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_raw)) %>%
  # Sort the data set by LibrarySize and create an Index to match the sorted data
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number())

# Visualize LibrarySize as a function of Index,
# to compare library size between samples
p_libsize <- ggplot(data = seq_depth,
                    aes(x = Index, y = LibrarySize, color = sample_type)) +
  geom_point()
p_libsize








# Save the plot in the figures folder. ggsave() saves a ggplot object; the file
# type is given by the extension (.png, .pdf, ...) and the size is in inches.
ggsave("figures/ITS/003_neg_library_size.png", p_libsize, width = 7, height = 5)

We can see that, compared to the rest of the samples, all controls have a small library size. If you zoom in on the lower left part of the plot (click and drag on the interactive plot above), you can see that the negative controls contain very few reads (1 to 19 reads), but they are not empty. Therefore, further analyses are required to know if the OTUs present in negative controls are contaminants.
Note that the positive controls (385 and 817 reads) have a larger library size than the negative controls, showing that sequencing performed well in these samples. This can be further confirmed in the previous section: Dealing with positive controls.
Furthermore, two samples have a very small library size compared to other samples (fewer reads than the positive controls). These samples should be further inspected to determine if their fungal community resembles that of other samples from the same site (i.e., replicates). If not, further investigation would be required to determine why these samples are different from other replicates: was there a methodological issue with these samples that resulted in the low sequencing depth; or is this a true biological exception that can occur among your replicates? When in doubt, ask those who collected and processed the samples.

Inspect samples with small library size

# Identify samples with a small library size
subset(seq_depth, sample_type == "sample" & LibrarySize < 1000) %>%
  select(SiteID, Soil_ID, Age, LibrarySize)

            SiteID Soil_ID Age LibrarySize
SNF4__29363 Oak_20  X29363  20         135
SNF4__29347 Oak_33  X29347  33         523


The samples SNF4__29363 (135 reads) and SNF4__29347 (523 reads) were taken on the sites Oak_20 and Oak_33. To compare them with their replicates: first, add a column to the sample data in the phyloseq object to identify these samples; then, visualize the samples in an ordination.

# Add a column to sample data in phyloseq object to identify these samples
sample_data(otu_table_raw)$low_depth <-
  sample_names(otu_table_raw) %in% c("SNF4__29363", "SNF4__29347")

# Plot an ordination of all samples to compare the low depth samples to replicates
p_low_depth_pcoa <- otu_table_raw %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "SiteID", shape = "low_depth", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = SiteID))
p_low_depth_pcoa









ggsave("figures/ITS/003_neg_low_depth_sample_pcoa.png", p_low_depth_pcoa,
       width = 7, height = 5)

These samples (shown with triangles) are located among the other samples of their site (Oak_20 and Oak_33) and the other oak forests. Their community composition is therefore similar to that of their replicates, and there is no reason to remove them at this stage. Note that the controls (NA, in gray) are located close to the oak forest samples: the few reads in the controls most likely come from the samples (see below).
However, their library size is very small: they will most likely be removed later, when choosing a rarefaction depth (see Rarefaction & normalization).



Prevalence of OTUs in negative controls

# For the following analyses, remove positive controls from the data set
otu_table_raw.noPos <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table_raw)$sample_type != "positive control", otu_table_raw)

First, visualize the prevalence of OTUs in samples and controls:

# Make phyloseq objects of presence-absence in controls and true samples
otu_table.pa <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_raw.noPos, function(x) 1*(x>0))
otu_table.pa.neg <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table.pa)$sample_type == "negative control", otu_table.pa)
otu_table.pa.sam <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table.pa)$sample_type == "sample", otu_table.pa)

# Make data.frame of prevalence in controls and true samples
otu_table.pa <- data.frame(pa.sam = taxa_sums(otu_table.pa.sam),
                           pa.neg = taxa_sums(otu_table.pa.neg))

# Plot the prevalence of OTU in negative controls vs true samples
p_prev <- ggplot(data=otu_table.pa, aes(x=pa.neg, y=pa.sam)) + geom_point() +
  xlab("Prevalence (Negative Controls)") + ylab("Prevalence (True Samples)")
p_prev









ggsave("figures/ITS/003_neg_prevalence_controls_vs_samples.png", p_prev,
       width = 7, height = 5)

37 OTUs are present in at least one negative control (‘Prevalence (Negative Controls)’ >= 1). Most of them are present in only one control, but in many true samples.
We must find out if there was a contamination in our samples from the method, or if the negative samples have been contaminated by the other samples.

# Convert OTU table from count data to relative abundance
otu_table_rel <- transform_sample_counts(
  otu_table_raw.noPos, function(x) x/sum(x))

# Identify OTUs present in negative controls
otu_neg <- filter(otu_table.pa, pa.neg > 0) %>% rownames()

# Filter OTU table to keep only OTUs found in negative controls
otu_table_neg <- prune_taxa(otu_neg, otu_table_rel)

# Visualize the abundance of these OTUs in all samples
p_neg_rel <- plot_bar(otu_table_neg, fill = "phylum") +
  facet_grid(~sample_type, scales = "free", space = "free")
p_neg_rel









ggsave("figures/ITS/003_neg_control_otus_relative_abundance.png", p_neg_rel,
       width = 12, height = 6)

A commonly recommended practice with negative controls is to remove any OTU found in negative controls from the rest of the data set[2]. However, as you can see in this demonstration, the OTUs found in the negative controls are found in all samples, and represent on average ~10% (and up to ~37%) of the community in the samples. Removing them would remove a large part of the fungal community. It is most likely that the OTUs found in the negative controls are present due to a contamination from the samples (e.g., during pipetting) and not the other way around.
Another way to confirm this, is to look at the count data instead of the relative abundance:

# Filter OTU table to keep only OTUs found in negative controls
otu_table_neg <- prune_taxa(otu_neg, otu_table_raw.noPos)

# Visualize the abundance of these OTUs in all samples
p_neg_counts <- plot_bar(otu_table_neg, fill = "phylum") +
  facet_grid(~sample_type, scales = "free", space = "free")
p_neg_counts









ggsave("figures/ITS/003_neg_control_otus_counts.png", p_neg_counts,
       width = 12, height = 6)

Here we can see that the abundance of these OTUs in the negative controls (1 to 19 reads) is very small compared to true samples (often hundreds of reads).
To deal with these OTUs and determine if they are truly contaminants, we can confirm (or infirm) our observations using the package decontam.



R package decontam
The R package decontam uses simple statistical tools to identify contaminants automatically[1]. Visit their webpage for more information.
In this demonstration, we use the function isContaminant with the prevalence method to find which OTUs are contaminants.

# First, add a TRUE/FALSE column "is.neg" to the sample_data
# to identify negative controls
sample_data(otu_table_raw.noPos)$is.neg <-
  sample_data(otu_table_raw.noPos)$sample_type == "negative control"

# Then use the function isContaminant with the default threshold = 0.1
contam.prev01 <- isContaminant(otu_table_raw.noPos, method="prevalence",
                               neg="is.neg", threshold = 0.1)

table(contam.prev01$contaminant)


FALSE  TRUE 
16687     4 


The method found 4 contaminant sequences at a threshold of 0.1 (default). In comparison, we had previously identified 37 OTUs present in the negative controls.
Increase the threshold to try and find more contaminants. This more aggressive threshold will identify as contaminants all sequences that are more prevalent in negative controls than in true samples.

# Use the function isContaminant with the more aggressive threshold = 0.5
contam.prev05 <- isContaminant(otu_table_raw.noPos, method="prevalence",
                               neg="is.neg", threshold = 0.5)

table(contam.prev05$contaminant)


FALSE  TRUE 
16674    17 


The method found 17 contaminant sequences at threshold = 0.5.

Inspect contaminants
Visualize the prevalence of these potential contaminants in samples and controls using the presence-absence table created earlier.

# Add a column to identify the contaminants found with each threshold
otu_table.pa <- mutate(otu_table.pa,
                       contaminant = case_when(
                         contam.prev01$contaminant ~ "threshold 0.1",
                         contam.prev05$contaminant ~ "threshold 0.5 only",
                         .default = "not a contaminant"))

# Plot the prevalence of OTU in negative controls vs true samples
p_prev_contam <- ggplot(data=otu_table.pa,
                        aes(x=pa.neg, y=pa.sam, color=contaminant)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("Prevalence (Negative Controls)") + ylab("Prevalence (True Samples)")
p_prev_contam









ggsave("figures/ITS/003_neg_prevalence_contaminants.png", p_prev_contam,
       width = 7, height = 5)

The negative controls contain so few reads that every OTU is present in at most 2 controls. With the threshold of 0.5, decontam also flags OTUs that are present in many true samples. Let’s look at the taxonomy of the flagged OTUs and at their number of reads in the true samples.

# Number of reads of each OTU in the true samples
otu_table_sam <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table_raw.noPos)$sample_type == "sample", otu_table_raw.noPos)

contam_check <- data.frame(
  tax_table(otu_table_raw.noPos)[, c("kingdom", "phylum", "genus")],
  reads_samples = taxa_sums(otu_table_sam),
  prevalence_samples = otu_table.pa$pa.sam,
  prevalence_controls = otu_table.pa$pa.neg,
  contaminant = otu_table.pa$contaminant) %>%
  filter(contaminant != "not a contaminant") %>%
  arrange(contaminant, desc(reads_samples))

The 4 OTUs flagged with the default threshold (0.1) have very few reads in the true samples (1 to 11 reads). One of them is Malassezia, a yeast living on human skin and a well-known laboratory contaminant. These are most likely true contaminants.
On the other hand, many of the additional OTUs flagged with the threshold of 0.5 are abundant in the true samples (up to ~600 reads), and some belong to typical soil and forest fungi, such as the ectomycorrhizal genera Cortinarius, Tomentella and Sebacina. These OTUs were most likely carried over from the samples into the negative controls, and removing them would remove real members of the fungal community. We therefore use the default threshold.

contaminants <- filter(contam.prev01, contaminant == TRUE) %>% rownames()

# Filter OTU table to keep only OTUs suspected of being contaminants
otu_table_contam <- prune_taxa(contaminants, otu_table_rel)

# Visualize the abundance of these OTUs in all samples
p_contam <- plot_bar(otu_table_contam, fill = "OTU") +
  facet_grid(~sample_type, scales = "free", space = "free") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_contam









ggsave("figures/ITS/003_neg_contaminants_relative_abundance.png", p_contam,
       width = 12, height = 6)

These OTUs make up a large part of the reads in the negative controls, and a negligible part of the reads in the true samples. It is safe to consider them as contaminants and remove them from the data set. The other OTUs present in the negative controls were most likely coming from true samples and are therefore not considered contaminants.






Note



With low-biomass controls such as these (few reads), decontam has little information to work with. Always inspect the flagged OTUs before removing them, as we did here. When in doubt, look into the taxonomy of the OTUs to determine if they are truly contaminants.





Clean and save OTU table
The two samples with a low sequencing depth (SNF4__29363 and SNF4__29347) are kept for now, as their community resembles that of their replicates.






Tipremove_taxa



Homemade function remove_taxa: a simplified way of removing a selection of OTU from a phyloseq object.

remove_taxa <- function(badTaxa, physeq){
  allTaxa <- taxa_names(physeq)
  cleanTaxa <- allTaxa[!(allTaxa %in% badTaxa)]
  return(prune_taxa(cleanTaxa, physeq))
}




# Remove contaminants (note that remove_taxa is a homemade function)
otu_ctrl_clean <- remove_taxa(contaminants, otu_table_raw)

# Remove all controls
otu_ctrl_clean <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_ctrl_clean)$sample_type != "positive control", otu_ctrl_clean)

otu_ctrl_clean <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_ctrl_clean)$sample_type != "negative control", otu_ctrl_clean)

# Save cleaned OTU table
save(otu_ctrl_clean, file = "RData/ITS/otu_ctrl_clean.RData")

title: Data preparation
text:
To get started with the data analysis, you must first ensure that the raw data is in the right format. This script shows an example on how to convert the raw data into a phyloseq object and produces the .RData files used in the next steps. More information about phyloseq can be found here.
To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 002_data_preparation.R and the example raw data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.



 


 Download script


 


 Download example raw data


 




Load auxiliary data
Auxiliary data files contain information about the samples and other types of environmental data. This example auxiliary data file contains site metadata and soil physicochemical analyses. Environmental data can be used in later analyses, such as db-RDA, while metadata can be used to filter samples in the phyloseq object.

# Load an Excel sheet (.xlsx)
aux <- read.xlsx("raw data/aux_data.xlsx")

# Load a text file (.txt or .csv)
aux <- read.csv("raw data/aux_data.csv")



Construct a phyloseq object from BLAST results
The procedure demonstrated below for ITS (fungi), the marker used in the examples of this website, can be applied similarly for the other target genes (16S and CO1). A complete procedure for each target gene can also be found in the downloadable script 002_data_preparation.R.

Taxonomy table
Our ITS taxonomy table was generated using BLASTn search against the UNITE database for fungi and other eukaryotes[1]. Make sure your taxonomy table looks similar to this one before continuing to the next steps. The BLAST results should contain BLAST quality measures (evalue, length, qcov, pident, etc.) for each OTU, and a taxonomy assignment. In this example, the taxonomy assignment is all contained in the same column “X1st_hit” and needs to be divided into BLAST_ID, kingdom, phylum, class, order, etc. After the species, the ITS taxonomy contains extra columns (x1, x2, …): for example, x1 tells whether the matched species is ectomycorrhizal (EcM) or not, and x3 gives the UNITE species hypothesis (SH) of the reference sequence. If the example shown here in R does not work with your raw file, you can try to do it in Excel (prone to errors). You may also find other example procedures to convert your raw data into a phyloseq object. More information about phyloseq can be found here.

# Load BLAST results
BLAST_raw <- read.delim("raw data/ITS_BLAST.txt")

# Verify that the data loaded properly: e.g., check that numeric value should 
# have class numeric or integer
summary(BLAST_raw)
View(BLAST_raw)







To extract taxonomy from BLAST results, transform the column “X1st_hit” into multiple columns: the BLAST ID (the identifier of the matched reference sequence), then one column per taxonomy level (kingdom, phylum, class, etc.), and clean the resulting table.

# Extract taxonomy from BLAST results
taxonomy_raw <- BLAST_raw %>%
  # Split columns based on delimiter (;)
  separate_wider_delim(cols = X1st_hit, delim = ";",
                       names = c("BLAST_ID","kingdom", "phylum", "class",
                                 "order", "family", "genus", "species", "x1",
                                 "x2", "x3", "x4", "x5", "x6", "x7", "x8", "x9",
                                 "x10", "x11", "x12"),
                       too_few = "align_start") %>%
  # Rename qseqid column to taxa_OTU
  as.data.frame() %>% dplyr::rename(taxa_OTU = qseqid) %>%
  # taxa_OTU names must be moved to row names
  `row.names<-`(.$taxa_OTU) %>%
  # Reorder columns: Make sure the largest grouping comes first (kingdom)
  relocate(any_of(c("query_seq", "taxa_OTU", "BLAST_ID")), .after = x12)



OTU table






CautionWere your samples part of a larger sequencing run containing other samples?



If your samples were mixed with multiple other samples in a larger library, you will need to filter your OTU table to keep only your own samples. You may then find OTUs present in none of your samples (they were present in the other samples you removed). Follow the procedure below to make sure to remove superfluous data before you proceed to the next scripts.


First load your OTU table and remove samples absent from your auxiliary data. Remember to include blanks, or negative and positive controls in your auxiliary data. Before proceeding to the next steps, make sure that the sample identifiers in your auxiliary file match those in the OTU table (column names).

# Load OTU table
otu_table_raw <- read.delim("raw data/ITS_table.txt")

# The first column contains OTU names, the rest are the count data per sample.

# Add sample identifier (Library_ID) as row names to aux data
row.names(aux) <- aux$Library_ID

# Clean the otu_table_raw to keep only relevant samples.
otu_table_raw <- otu_table_raw %>%
  # Keep only samples from aux data
  select(OTU, contains(rownames(aux))) %>%
  # OTU names must be moved to row names
  as.data.frame() %>% `row.names<-`(.$OTU) %>% select(!OTU)

After cleaning the OTU table, make sure the selected columns match your auxiliary data. Potentially missing samples may have not amplified properly and were removed during bioinformatic processing. Ask your lab technician or the company providing your sequences for more information about missing samples.


Format the data into a phyloseq-class object
Combine your OTU table, auxiliary data and taxonomy table into a phyloseq-class object. For more information about phyloseq, look up[2], or their GitHub pages.

# Combine data into a phyloseq-class object
otu_table_raw <- phyloseq(otu_table(otu_table_raw, taxa_are_rows = T),
                          sample_data(aux),
                          tax_table(as.matrix(taxonomy_raw)))

Were your samples part of a larger sequencing run containing other samples? Filter out OTU absent from your data set.

# Remove all OTUs with sum == 0
ntaxa(otu_table_raw) # 27701 before filtering
otu_table_raw <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_table_raw) > 0, otu_table_raw)
ntaxa(otu_table_raw) # 16691 after filtering

40% of the OTUs were absent from this subset of samples.



Save as .RData
Save all newly created files as RData for usage with other scripts.

save(BLAST_raw, file = "RData/ITS/BLAST_raw.RData")
save(taxonomy_raw, file = "RData/ITS/taxonomy_raw.RData")
save(otu_table_raw, file = "RData/ITS/otu_table_raw.RData")
save(aux, file = "RData/auxfile.RData")

Now that the data is ready, take a first look at it: Explore the data.





References

1. Abarenkov, K., Nilsson, R. H., Larsson, K.-H., et al. (2024). The UNITE database for molecular identification and taxonomic communication of fungi and other eukaryotes: Sequences, taxa and classifications reconsidered. Nucleic Acids Research, 52(D1), D791–D797. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkad1039


2. McMurdie, P. J., & Holmes, S. (2013). Phyloseq: An r package for reproducible interactive analysis and graphics of microbiome census data. PLoS ONE, 8(4), e61217. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0061217

title: Microbiome analysis workflow
text:
This workflow was created for microbiome analyses within the Silva Nova project, to ensure that all publications related to the Silva Nova project use the same data processing, and avoid inconsistencies between sub-projects. This workflow should also make microbial analyses more accessible and streamlined.
The examples on this website use the ITS (fungi) data set of the Silva Nova project, and translate the analyses of the Silva Nova PhD course “Forest microbial ecology and eDNA” to phyloseq objects. An earlier version of this website, based on the 16S (bacteria) data set, is kept as an archive in the GitHub repository (folder website-16S).
Decisions for each step of the workflow are supported by literature and R scripts, which aim to answer the following questions:

title: Microbiome analysis workflow
text:
Structure
In the navigation menu of this webpage, you will find each step of the workflow:

Get started

Install R and required packages: get started with RStudio and install the packages required for the analyses in this workflow
Data preparation: prepare OTU tables, manage metadata, and convert raw files to .RData
Explore the data: take a first look at samples, OTUs, reads and taxonomy

Handling OTU tables

Controls: deal with OTUs found in negative and positive controls
Filtering: filter out OTUs based on abundance and prevalence, or based on taxonomy and BLAST quality
Rarefaction and normalization: rarefy or transform data to control for variable sequencing depth

Statistical analyses

Alpha diversity: choose the best alpha diversity metrics to answer your hypothesis
Taxonomic composition and guilds: visualize the taxonomic composition and the fungal guilds of the communities
Beta diversity: choose the right transformation and the right distance matrix for beta diversity analyses
Indicator species: find the taxa associated with groups of samples
RDA and variation partitioning: relate community composition to environmental variables

title: Handling OTU tables
text:
Before any statistical analysis, the raw OTU tables must be cleaned so that the downstream results reflect the true biological signal rather than technical noise. The steps below should be applied in the order presented, since each script loads the phyloseq object saved by the previous one (e.g., otu_ctrl_clean → otu_rare_clean → otu_BLAST_clean).






TipStart from the data preparation step



All scripts in this section assume that your raw data has already been converted to a phyloseq object and saved as .RData. If this is not the case, go through Data preparation first, and make sure that the required packages are installed and loaded.



Dealing with controls
Negative controls, blanks and positive controls are used to verify that the full workflow (from DNA extraction to bioinformatics) behaved as expected. Inspect them, remove contaminants, and then remove the controls themselves from the data set.

Dealing with positive controls: identify the synthetic community and confirm that taxonomic profiles match expectations
Dealing with negative controls (and blanks): inspect library sizes, find contaminants with the R package decontam, and remove low-quality samples



Filtering OTU tables
Remove OTUs that are artefacts or that cannot be reliably identified, and clean the taxonomic assignations.

Global filtering

Taxonomy filtering: keep only the organisms targeted by the primers
Singletons and rare OTUs: remove OTUs based on absolute or relative abundance thresholds

BLAST quality check

BLAST filtering: remove short or poorly aligned sequences
BLAST cleaning: remove unknown organisms and replace low-confidence taxonomic assignations with NA




Rarefaction and normalization
Account for differing sequencing depths across samples before comparing communities.

Rarefaction: draw rarefaction curves, choose a sufficient depth, and check whether library sizes are balanced between groups
Transformations: alternatives that preserve all reads, such as relative abundance, Hellinger, CLR and robust CLR







TipDownload all scripts



Each page of this section offers a download button for its own script and example data. All pre-made scripts can also be downloaded at once from the home page.

title: Dealing with positive controls
text:
This section documents how to inspect positive controls to confirm successful amplification of target genes, detect false results, and overall, verify that the full workflow (from extraction to bioinformatics) behaves as expected[1].
To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 003_positive_control.R and the example raw data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.



 


 Download script


 


 Download example RData


 




Inspect samples
Positive controls added before sequencing usually contain a synthetic community (OTUs absent from true samples) and serve to demonstrate successful amplification of target genes or provide information about tag-switching. In this example, the positive controls contain a synthetic ITS sequence (a “spike-in”), which is assigned to the kingdom Unispike1 in the taxonomy table.

# Load raw OTU table
load("RData/ITS/otu_table_raw.RData")

To inspect this data set, convert OTU table from count data to both a presence-absence table and a relative abundance table.

# Convert OTU table from count data to presence-absence
otu_table.pa <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_raw, function(x) 1*(x>0))

# Convert OTU table from count data to relative abundance
otu_table.rel <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_raw, function(x) x/sum(x))


Identify synthetic community

# Identify OTUs present in positive controls
otu_table.pa.pos <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table.pa)$sample_type == "positive control", otu_table.pa)

table.pa.pos <- data.frame(pa.pos = taxa_sums(otu_table.pa.pos))

otu_pos <- filter(table.pa.pos, pa.pos > 0) %>% rownames()

# Filter OTU table to keep only OTUs found in positive controls
otu_table_pos <- prune_taxa(otu_pos, otu_table.rel)

# Visualize the abundance of these OTUs in all samples
p_pos_otus <- plot_bar(otu_table_pos, fill = "kingdom") +
  facet_grid(~sample_type, scales = "free", space = "free")
p_pos_otus









# Save the plot in the figures folder
ggsave("figures/ITS/003_pos_control_otus_relative_abundance.png", p_pos_otus,
       width = 12, height = 6)

Nearly all reads in the two positive controls (385 and 817 reads) belong to the spike-in (Unispike1), as expected. The positive controls also contain a few reads (1 to 2 per OTU) of soil fungi, such as the ectomycorrhizal genera Cortinarius and Inocybe, which most likely come from the true samples. These cross-contaminations can be dealt with using the R package decontam, as demonstrated in the next section: Dealing with negative controls.
The spike-in is absent from the true samples, so there was no contamination from the positive controls into the samples. The spike-in will be automatically removed from our data set while performing taxonomic filtering, which keeps only Fungi.


Compare community profiles
If one suspects issues with library preparation or sequencing, positive controls can be used for visual inspection, by making sure the taxonomic profiles match expectations.

# Keep only positive controls for visualization
otu_table.rel.pos <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table.rel)$sample_type == "positive control", otu_table.rel)

# Visualize the community profiles of these samples
p_pos_profiles <- plot_bar(otu_table.rel.pos, fill = "kingdom")
p_pos_profiles









ggsave("figures/ITS/003_pos_control_profiles.png", p_pos_profiles,
       width = 7, height = 5)

Both positive controls show the same profile, dominated by the spike-in: no obvious issue was detected during library preparation or sequencing.



Clean and save OTU table
Since no issue was detected, the positive controls can simply be removed from the data set.

Homemade function remove_taxa: a simplified way of removing a selection of OTU from a phyloseq object.

remove_taxa <- function(badTaxa, physeq){
  allTaxa <- taxa_names(physeq)
  cleanTaxa <- allTaxa[!(allTaxa %in% badTaxa)]
  return(prune_taxa(cleanTaxa, physeq))
}




# Remove positive controls
otu_ctrl_pos_clean <- prune_samples(
  sample_data(otu_table_raw)$sample_type != "positive control", otu_table_raw)

# Save cleaned OTU table
save(otu_ctrl_pos_clean, file = "RData/ITS/otu_ctrl_pos_clean.RData")

title: Filtering OTU tables
text:
This section presents three important ways of cleaning the OTU tables:
The two downloadable scripts below (004_global_filter.R and 005_BLAST_filter.R) implement a standard approach for cleaning OTU tables based on taxonomy, abundance and prevalence, or based on BLAST quality, in a phyloseq object.
Download script 004_global_filter


 


 Download script 005_BLAST_filter
For a step-by-step explanation of each filtering procedure, see the sections below:

title: Filtering OTU tables
text:
Global filtering
A global filtering - based on taxonomic assignations, abundance of OTUs across all samples (singletons and rare features), or based on the prevalence of OTUs across samples (scarcity) - is typically applied early to remove very low-count and low-prevalence features that are disproportionately driven by sequencing/PCR error and index misassignment, thereby reducing noise and improving downstream compositional and multivariate analyses.

Taxonomy filtering
This first simple step serves to target only the relevant OTUs that were targeted with each primer sets: i.e., Bacteria for 16S, Fungi for ITS and Metazoa for CO1.


Singletons and rare OTUs
Singleton OTUs have been shown to be overwhelmingly composed of artefacts arising from PCR and sequencing errors, including chimeric molecules that are typically low-abundance and sample-restricted[5,6]. Their removal has repeatedly been shown to have negligible effects on hypothesis-driven community comparisons while substantially reducing noise[1,2,7]. On the other hand, retaining them is justifiable in studies explicitly targeting rare biosphere diversity, but requires careful manual curation[3].
Rare OTUs (beyond singletons) can hardly be distinguished from artefacts, thus, low-abundance OTUs are often excluded from the analysis. However, filtering approaches vary among studies, and there is no agreed-upon consensus as to what filtering thresholds should be employed[2,8,9]. Nevertheless, rare OTUs, just like singletons, often represent residual artefacts, and removing them has minimal influence on community comparisons. Thus, filtering reduces the complexity of microbiome data while preserving their integrity in downstream analysis[1,2,7,10]. Although rare taxa may in some contexts carry information on beta diversity, their retention is mainly justified in studies explicitly focused on rare biosphere ecology, where careful validation is required[3].
Rare OTUs are frequently removed using absolute abundance thresholds (e.g. <5 or <10 reads)[3,7], or based on relative abundance thresholds (e.g. <0.01%)[2], while others filter rare OTUs based on statistical methods[11].


Scarce OTUs
Scarce (low-prevalence) OTUs are features detected in only a small fraction of samples (<5%). The extreme sparsity of microbiome data sets poses a major analytical challenge and is largely attributable to sequencing artefacts, contamination, and/or sequencing errors[10]. Thus, scarce OTUs are commonly filtered using simple rule-of-thumb criteria (e.g. presence in at least k samples or k% of samples), which reduces noise and improves statistical stability[10]. This criterion does not relate to the relative abundance of the OTUs, and as such, rare OTUs may be prevalent microbial taxa.
In certain studies, higher thresholds for prevalence (>25% of samples) may be used to define, for instance, the core microbiome[12].
In the ITS example of this workflow, the thresholds are compared, but all fungal OTUs are kept: rare OTUs and singletons are needed to estimate the extrapolated richness (alpha diversity), and the low sequencing depth of the data set makes even the lowest thresholds remove a large proportion of the OTUs.

title: Filtering OTU tables
text:
BLAST quality check
Filtering based on BLAST accuracy is applied to remove OTUs with low-confidence taxonomic assignments, typically indicated by low sequence similarity (pident), poor alignment coverage (qcovs), or poor fit of the rank resolution (evalue)[4]. Such features are frequently artefactual or biologically uninterpretable and can bias ecological inference if retained.

BLAST filtering
Filtering out OTUs based on BLAST results is normally done during bioinformatic processing, but if it was not the case for your OTU table, simple filters can be used to further remove artefacts. For instance, sequences that are too short (e.g., <100 bp for ITS or <250 bp for 16S, depending on primers) to be a proper amplicon, or sequences with less than 15% query coverage (qcovs), which are assumed to be fully synthetic[13].


BLAST cleaning
After filtering out any remaining potential artefacts, BLAST statistics (such as pident and evalue) can also be used to confirm taxonomic assignments. There is a lack of objective criteria (such as numerical thresholds) for taxonomic assignations of uncultured microorganisms, which are identified only by sequence data. Few studies have attempted to determine universal thresholds for each taxonomic group: some have determined some completely arbitrary rule of thumb[14], and others have identified thresholds that can be applied in specific cases[5,15–18].

title: Global filtering
text:
A global filtering is typically applied early to preserve only relevant taxonomic assignations and remove very low-count OTUs that are disproportionately driven by sequencing/PCR error and index misassignment, thereby reducing noise and improving downstream compositional and multivariate analyses.
This section documents how to filter OTUs based on taxonomic assignations, how to explore the abundance and prevalence of OTUs, and how to filter out singletons and rare OTUs based on absolute or relative abundance thresholds in phyloseq objects. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 004_global_filter.R and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

title: Global filtering
text:
Taxonomy filtering
This first simple step serves to preserve only the relevant OTUs that were targeted with each primer sets: i.e., Bacteria for 16S, Fungi for ITS and Metazoa for CO1.
Note that the 16S primers amplifying the V4-V5 regions are also suitable for Archaea. The choice to include them or not in the following filtering depends on the hypotheses of your study. Similarly, primers targeting the internal transcribed spacer (ITS1 and ITS2) regions, while commonly used as the universal barcoding marker for fungi, often co-amplify DNA from a wide variety of other Eukaryotes due to the conserved nature of the flanking ribosomal RNA genes (18S, 5.8S, and 28S). For example, DNA from plants and protists is often amplified using these primers. It is recommended to filter them out when the hypotheses of the study are focused on Fungi. Finally, CO1 primers may also amplify Prokaryotes or other Eukaryotes, but these are not specificly targeted and should be filtered out.

# Select organisms that should be included in the analysis
otu_table_tax <- subset_taxa(otu_ctrl_clean, kingdom == "Fungi")

# Count OTUs before and after filtering
ntaxa(otu_ctrl_clean) # 16687
ntaxa(otu_table_tax) # 9043 (~46% of the OTUs were not Fungi)

In this demonstration, ~46% of the OTUs (and ~16% of the reads) were not Fungi. The ITS primers also amplify many other eukaryotes (e.g., Alveolata, Rhizaria, Amoebozoa, Metazoa and plants), as well as the synthetic spike-in of the positive controls (kingdom Unispike1, see Dealing with positive controls). These are all removed here.
Which organisms to preserve or to remove from your data set depends on your sample type (e.g., soil vs water), the origin of your sample (e.g., tropical vs arctic) and your research question. Note that each genetic marker needs its own taxonomy filter. For example, the 16S primers also amplify chloroplasts and mitochondria, which contain DNA similar to bacteria because they are ancestral bacteria. In the databases used to BLAST the 16S marker, chloroplasts are assigned at the order level and mitochondria at the family level, both within the kingdom Bacteria, and must be removed separately:

# 16S only: remove chloroplasts and mitochondria
otu_table_tax <- subset_taxa(otu_ctrl_clean, kingdom == "Bacteria")
otu_table_tax <- subset_taxa(otu_table_tax, order != "Chloroplast" &
                               family != "Mitochondria")

title: Global filtering
section: Explore the abundance and prevalence of OTUs
text:
Explore the abundance and prevalence of OTUs
Sequencing data sets are characterized by a long tail of rare OTUs, i.e., OTUs represented by a low number of reads. Some of them may be products of sequencing errors that were not removed by the bioinformatic pipeline. Are they real? Is their presence meaningful in our analysis? It is often hard to decide which cutoff to use for an OTU to be considered “real”, and the choice is often a bit arbitrary. It is therefore important to explore the data before deciding.

Number of reads per OTU
Some OTUs have 0 reads at this stage: they were only present in the control samples, which were removed in the previous step. We exclude them from the exploration.

# Remove the OTUs with 0 reads (only present in the controls)
otu_table_explore <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_table_tax) > 0, otu_table_tax)

# Total number of reads per OTU
reads_otu <- data.frame(reads = taxa_sums(otu_table_explore))

min(reads_otu$reads) # 1 read
max(reads_otu$reads) # 16793 reads

# How many OTUs have more than 1000 reads?
sum(reads_otu$reads > 1000) # 58 OTUs


# Plot the distribution of the number of reads per OTU (log scale)
ggplot(reads_otu, aes(x = reads)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Number of reads per OTU (log10 scale)", y = "Number of OTUs") +
  theme_minimal()








Most OTUs have a low number of reads, and only a few OTUs (58) are very abundant, with more than 1000 reads.


Prevalence of OTUs
The prevalence of an OTU is the number of samples in which it is present. To calculate it, we first convert the OTU table to presence-absence.

# Convert the OTU table to presence-absence (1 = present, 0 = absent)
otu_table_pa <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_explore, function(x) 1 * (x > 0))

# Number of OTUs per sample
sample_sums(otu_table_pa)

# Number of samples in which each OTU is present (prevalence)
prev_otu <- data.frame(prevalence = taxa_sums(otu_table_pa))

# How many OTUs are present in only one or two samples?
sum(prev_otu$prevalence == 1) # 4843 OTUs
sum(prev_otu$prevalence == 2) # 1367 OTUs


# Plot the distribution of the prevalence of OTUs
ggplot(prev_otu, aes(x = prevalence)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Prevalence of OTUs (number of samples)", y = "Number of OTUs") +
  theme_minimal()








Most OTUs occur in a very low number of samples: more than half of the fungal OTUs (4843) are found in a single sample. Filtering OTUs based on their prevalence would therefore lead to the loss of a large number of OTUs.
What if we remove the OTUs present in less than 10 samples?

# Keep the OTUs present in at least 10 samples
prev_otu10 <- filter(prev_otu, prevalence >= 10)

ggplot(prev_otu10, aes(x = prevalence)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Prevalence of OTUs (number of samples)", y = "Number of OTUs") +
  theme_minimal()








Even after removing the OTUs present in less than 10 samples, the same pattern is observed: OTUs with a low prevalence are the most frequent. It is hard to choose a cutoff based on prevalence only. Let’s look at filters based on the abundance of OTUs instead.

title: Global filtering
text:
Singletons and rare OTUs
Singletons and other rare OTUs are predominantly composed of PCR, sequencing, and chimera artefacts, and their removal has been shown to have negligible effects on hypothesis-driven community comparisons while substantially reducing noise[5–8]. Retaining them is mainly justified in studies explicitly targeting rare biosphere diversity and requires careful validation[9].
In R, singletons are typically removed by excluding OTUs with a total count of one across all samples, while rare OTUs are filtered by applying absolute (e.g. total counts <5 or <10) or relative abundance thresholds (e.g. <0.01%) to the OTU table[5,6,9], commonly using phyloseq::prune_taxa() in combination with taxa_sums().

Removing singletons
Removing singletons is as simple as keeping anything that has more than 1 read throughout the entire data set.

# Remove singletons
otu_table_single <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_table_tax) > 1, otu_table_tax)

# Count OTUs after filtering
ntaxa(otu_table_single) # 5825 (~36% of the fungal OTUs were singletons)

In this data set, a large proportion of the OTUs (~36%) are singletons, i.e., OTUs with a single read in the whole data set. Together, however, they represent less than 1% of the reads.


Removing rare OTUs
OTUs are considered rare if their abundance is small compared to other OTUs. They may be present in many samples, but if their total sum across samples is smaller than k% of the average sequencing depth (relative abundance), or smaller than k reads (absolute abundance) then they are considered rare.
NOTE: When calculating the average sequencing depth, ignore controls and blanks, as they artificially lower the average.

Relative abundance
Typically, thresholds between 0.005% and 0.1% relative abundance are found in the literature. We define relative thresholds based on the average sequencing depth (assuming that all samples have sufficient sequencing depth).

# Calculate the average sequencing depth
seq_depth_avg <- mean(sample_sums(otu_table_tax)) # 4048.7 reads

# Calculate thresholds based on k% of the average sequencing depth
# For the sake of this exercise, multiple thresholds between 0.05% and 1% are
# tested to compare their effects on various community analyses.
thresh05 <- ceiling(seq_depth_avg*0.05/100) # 3 reads
thresh1 <- ceiling(seq_depth_avg*0.1/100) # 5 reads
thresh10 <- ceiling(seq_depth_avg*1/100) # 41 reads

Because the sequencing depth of this ITS data set is low (~4000 reads per sample), the lower thresholds found in the literature (0.005% or 0.01%) correspond to 1 read, i.e., they are identical to removing singletons. For the sake of this demonstration, we have therefore tested thresholds of 0.05% and 0.1%, as well as a threshold up to 1% to better illustrate the effects of filtering out rare OTUs on different community analyses. With a deeper sequencing (e.g., ~140000 reads per sample, typical of 16S data sets), the same percentages correspond to many more reads (0.005% = 7 reads, 0.01% = 14 reads).

# Remove all OTUs that have a total sum lower than the threshold
otu_table_rare05 <- otu_table_tax %>% prune_taxa(taxa_sums(.) > thresh05, .)
otu_table_rare1 <- otu_table_tax %>% prune_taxa(taxa_sums(.) > thresh1, .)
otu_table_rare10 <- otu_table_tax %>% prune_taxa(taxa_sums(.) > thresh10, .)

# Compare the number of OTU in each filtering step
ntaxa(otu_ctrl_clean) #16687 (before filtering)
ntaxa(otu_table_tax) #9043 (~54% of OTUs are Fungi)
ntaxa(otu_table_single) #5825 (~36% singletons)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare05) #3597 (~60% of OTUs have 3 reads or less; 0.05%)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare1) #2763 (~69% of OTUs have 5 reads or less; 0.1%)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare10) #787 (~91% of OTUs have 41 reads or less; 1%)



Absolute abundance
Typically, thresholds between 5-10 reads are found in the literature. In this example, a threshold of 5 reads corresponds to a relative abundance threshold of 0.1%. If the average sequencing depth of your data set is larger than the one presented here, it may be relevant to test removing 5 and 10 reads if those absolute thresholds are significantly lower than a relative threshold at 0.005%.


Compare thresholds
To visualize the effect of these different thresholds, we must first create a data frame per filtered OTU table that summarizes the sequencing depth per sample and the Observed OTU (richness).

# Non-filtered OTU table
seq_depth_raw <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_tax)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_tax, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_tax)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "raw")

# Singletons
seq_depth_single <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_single)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_single, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_single)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "singletons")

# Rare 0.05% (<=3 reads)
seq_depth_rare05 <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rare05)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_rare05, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_rare05)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "rare 0.05%")

# Rare 0.1% (<=5 reads)
seq_depth_rare1 <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rare1)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_rare1, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_rare1)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "rare 0.1%")

# Rare 1% (<=41 reads)
seq_depth_rare10 <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rare10)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_rare10, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_rare10)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "rare 1%")

# Combine data frames
seq_depth_all <- seq_depth_raw %>% rbind(seq_depth_single) %>%
  rbind(seq_depth_rare05) %>% rbind(seq_depth_rare1) %>%
  rbind(seq_depth_rare10)


Effect on library size

# Plot the library size of all samples
ggplot(seq_depth_all, aes(x = Index, y = LibrarySize, color = seq_depth)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line()







With this analysis, we can see that removing singletons barely affects library size, as the points almost completely overlap with the non-filtered data, even though we lost ~36% of the OTUs. In addition, filtering rare OTUs at a threshold of 0.1% or less (5 reads or less) changes very little in the library size, even though we lost ~69% of the OTUs. Only the threshold of 1% removes a substantial number of reads.






Tip



Try zooming in on a selection of points with large library size (e.g., the samples with an Index above 80) to better see the effects of the different thresholds.




Effect on OTU richness
To confirm our choice of the best filtering threshold, let’s compare the effect of filtering on OTU richness.

# Plot the OTU richness of all samples
ggplot(seq_depth_all, aes(x = Index, y = Observed, color = seq_depth)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line()







This plot shows that every filtering step lowers the OTU richness of the samples, especially in the samples with a large library size. The thresholds up to 0.1% return the same pattern of OTU richness as a function of library size, whereas the threshold of 1% flattens the differences between samples.






Tip



Try comparing other alpha diversity indices, such as the Shannon index.

# Add Shannon index to each OTU table as such
seq_depth_raw <- seq_depth_raw %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_tax, measures = "Shannon"))

# Plot the Shannon index of all samples
ggplot(seq_depth_all, aes(x = Index, y = Shannon, color = seq_depth)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line()







Filtering rare OTUs has little effect on the Shannon index, which gives more weight to abundant OTUs. Note also the lack of a clear relationship between the Shannon index and library size.




Effect on beta diversity
To confirm our choice of filtering further, we can compare how the different filtering methods affect beta diversity.

# Non-filtered OTU table
beta_div_raw <- otu_table_tax %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Singletons
beta_div_single <- otu_table_single %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Rare 0.05%
beta_div_rare05 <- otu_table_rare05 %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Rare 0.1%
beta_div_rare1 <- otu_table_rare1 %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Rare 1%
beta_div_rare10 <- otu_table_rare10 %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Visualize all plots together
ggarrange(beta_div_raw, beta_div_single, beta_div_rare05, beta_div_rare1,
          beta_div_rare10,
          labels = c(
            "Non-filtered (9043 OTUs)", "Singletons (5825 OTUs)",
            "0.05% (<=3 reads; 3597 OTUs)", "0.1% (<=5 reads; 2763 OTUs)",
            "1% (<=41 reads; 787 OTUs)"),
          ncol = 3, nrow = 2, common.legend = TRUE,
          hjust = 0, label.x = 0.2, font.label = list(size = 10))








With this analysis, we can see that the overall patterns are the same with all filtering thresholds: the agricultural sites and the grassland separate from the oak forests. Note that the orientation of the axes is arbitrary: an axis may simply be flipped from one plot to the other.
Overall, these plots showed that rare OTUs were mostly found in samples with a large library size, and that filtering out rare OTUs does not affect the main patterns. Only a threshold as high as 1% considerably affected the richness of the samples.



Choosing the best threshold
Ultimately, the choice of the “best” threshold is completely arbitrary. Various thresholds are found in the literature and no one is more justified than another. As a reminder: singletons and other rare OTUs have been previously found to be predominantly composed of artefacts, thus, their removal has been shown to have negligible effects on hypothesis-driven community comparisons while substantially reducing noise[5–8]. Retaining them is only justified in studies explicitly targeting rare biosphere diversity and requires careful validation[9].
So, is it necessary to filter rare OTUs? As seen in this demonstration, removing rare OTUs mainly lowers the richness of the samples, and has little effect on the community composition. In this workflow, we keep all fungal OTUs (no abundance filter), for two reasons:

Rare OTUs, and singletons in particular, are needed to estimate the number of undetected OTUs in each sample (extrapolated richness, see Alpha diversity). Removing them would bias these estimates.
The sequencing depth of this data set is low, so that even the lowest thresholds remove a large proportion of the OTUs.

We only remove the OTUs with 0 reads (only present in the controls).

# Keep all fungal OTUs, but remove the OTUs with 0 reads
otu_table_rare <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_table_tax) > 0, otu_table_tax)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare) # 9039 OTUs

To use a filtering threshold instead, replace the line above with, e.g., otu_table_rare <- otu_table_single (remove singletons) or otu_table_rare <- otu_table_rare05 (remove OTUs with 3 reads or less).






Important



If you decide to filter rare OTUs in your own data, report the threshold you used, and check that it does not change your conclusions.





Save the OTU tables

# OTU table with taxonomy filtered
save(otu_table_tax, file = "RData/ITS/otu_taxa_clean.RData")

# OTU table with singletons filtered
save(otu_table_single, file = "RData/ITS/otu_single_clean.RData")

# OTU table with rare taxa filtered
save(otu_table_rare, file = "RData/ITS/otu_rare_clean.RData")

title: Statistical Analyses
text:
Once the OTU tables are cleaned and normalized (see Handling OTU tables), the communities can be described and compared. Each script in this section loads the OTU table filtered with BLAST (otu_BLAST_clean.RData) and standardizes it as shown in Rarefaction and normalization.

Alpha diversity
Compare the diversity within samples (richness, Shannon and Simpson diversity) between groups, using rarefied data or rarefaction/extrapolation curves (iNEXT).


Taxonomic composition and guilds
Visualize the relative abundance of the main taxa and fungal guilds in each group of samples.


Beta diversity
Compare the composition of communities between samples: transformations and distances (Hellinger and Bray-Curtis, Aitchison, Jaccard), ordinations (PCoA), and tests (PERMANOVA, homogeneity of dispersions).


Indicator species
Find the taxa that are associated with groups of samples (indicator species analysis).


RDA and variation partitioning
Relate community composition to environmental variables with redundancy analysis (RDA), and quantify the variation explained by groups of variables.

title: Beta diversity
text:
Beta diversity quantifies how different the taxonomic composition of two samples is. It is calculated as a distance (or dissimilarity) between each pair of samples. Several distance metrics exist, and each of them emphasises different aspects of the communities: the abundant OTUs, the rare OTUs, or only their presence or absence. The choice of the metric can change the interpretation of the data, as shown below.
This section documents how to calculate distance matrices with three metrics (Bray-Curtis, Aitchison and Jaccard), how to visualise them with a Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA), and how to test differences between groups of samples with PERMANOVA and the homogeneity of group dispersions. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script 020_beta_diversity.R and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.
Download script


 


 Download example RData
To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see BLAST filtering), and set the seed for the rarefaction and the permutation tests. We also order the land uses from agriculture to the old forest, for the plots and tables.
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
set.seed(100)

sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use <- factor(
  sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use,
  levels = c("Conventional agriculture", "Organic agriculture", "Grassland",
             "Oak", "Old Ref"))

title: Beta diversity
text:
Data transformation
Metabarcoding data are compositional: the number of reads does not reflect the total abundance of the fungi in the soil, only the relative abundances within a sample can be compared. The data also contain a long tail of rare OTUs: a few OTUs are very abundant and most are rare. The data must therefore be transformed before calculating distances (see also Rarefaction & normalization).

Rarefied data and Hellinger transformation
As in Alpha diversity, we start from the data rarefied to 1011 reads (same seed, so the same rarefied table).

otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, sample.size = 1011,
                                      replace = FALSE, rngseed = 100,
                                      verbose = FALSE)
nsamples(otu_table_rarefy)

[1] 87

ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)

[1] 5153

# Check: all samples should have 1011 reads
summary(sample_sums(otu_table_rarefy))

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   1011    1011    1011    1011    1011    1011 


The Hellinger transformation is the square root of the relative abundances[1]. Dividing by the sample total converts the counts to relative abundances, and the square root gives less weight to the few very abundant OTUs (it stabilises the variance).

otu_table_hel <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_rarefy,
                                         function(x) sqrt(x / sum(x)))



CLR transformation of the non-rarefied data
The Aitchison distance is calculated on the non-rarefied data (all 89 samples), after a centred log-ratio (CLR) transformation: the log of each count minus the mean of the logs of the sample. The log of 0 is not defined, so a pseudocount of 1 is added to all counts (as in Rarefaction & normalization).

otu_table_clr <- transform_sample_counts(otu_BLAST_clean, function(x) {
  lx <- log(x + 1)
  lx - mean(lx)
})

We also keep the metadata of the samples for the plots and tests below.

meta_rare <- data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rarefy)) # 87 samples
meta_all  <- data.frame(sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean))  # 89 samples

title: Beta diversity
text:
Distance matrices
Each distance metric emphasises different aspects of the communities:

Bray-Curtis: abundance-based, dominated by the abundant OTUs. Here it is calculated on the Hellinger-transformed rarefied data.
Aitchison: the Euclidean distance between centred log-ratio (CLR) transformed abundances. It is designed for compositional data[2], and does not need rarefied data. The log of 0 is not defined, so a small constant (pseudocount) is added to all counts.
Jaccard: presence-absence only (binary = TRUE), the abundances are ignored. Calculated on the rarefied data.

Other metrics exist, e.g. UniFrac, which uses the phylogenetic relationships between OTUs. It is not available for ITS, which cannot be aligned across all fungi.

# Bray-Curtis dissimilarities on the Hellinger-transformed data
dist_bray <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_hel, method = "bray")
head(dist_bray)

[1] 0.4641830 0.4473362 0.4531600 0.4628954 0.5026855 0.4175194

# Aitchison distances: the Euclidean distances between the CLR-transformed
# samples
dist_ait <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_clr, method = "euclidean")
head(dist_ait)

[1] 21.94361 22.67389 22.95505 22.50210 23.19787 20.52029

# Jaccard distances on the rarefied data (presence-absence)
dist_jac <- phyloseq::distance(otu_table_rarefy, method = "jaccard",
                               binary = TRUE)
head(dist_jac)

[1] 0.7020548 0.6887417 0.6968641 0.7000000 0.7350158 0.6600000








Note



phyloseq has no Aitchison distance, but the Euclidean distance on CLR data computed above gives exactly the same result as the vegan version, vegdist(otu_mat, method = "aitchison", pseudocount = 1), where otu_mat is the OTU matrix with the samples as rows.
The tutorial of the course uses the robust Aitchison distance instead, which only uses the non-zero counts, without adding a pseudocount (see Rarefaction & normalization). Both are valid. The robust version is not available in phyloseq: it is calculated with vegan, e.g. vegdist(otu_mat, method = "robust.aitchison"), on the OTU matrix extracted from the phyloseq object. From that step on, the analysis would continue outside phyloseq.
With a pseudocount, absent OTUs and OTUs with very few reads get similar values, which is important to interpret the PCoA below.

title: Beta diversity
text:
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA)
A distance matrix contains one value for each pair of samples (87 samples: 3741 pairs), too many to look at. An ordination such as the Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) summarises the distances in a few axes, so that similar samples are close to each other in the plot. phyloseq::ordinate() runs the PCoA with ape::pcoa().

pcoa_bray <- ordinate(otu_table_hel, method = "PCoA", distance = dist_bray)
pcoa_ait  <- ordinate(otu_table_clr, method = "PCoA", distance = dist_ait)
pcoa_jac  <- ordinate(otu_table_rarefy, method = "PCoA", distance = dist_jac)

# Proportion of the variation explained by the first axes
head(pcoa_bray$values$Relative_eig)

[1] 0.17317796 0.06191143 0.05781331 0.04437245 0.03880940 0.03291946

head(pcoa_ait$values$Relative_eig)

[1] 0.15849611 0.06757338 0.06000608 0.04450282 0.03662090 0.03194578

head(pcoa_jac$values$Relative_eig)

[1] 0.09752194 0.03790395 0.03637536 0.02917491 0.02754256 0.02418366



Plot
The three PCoA plots use the same code, so we write it in a function. plot_pcoa() draws the samples on the first two axes, coloured by site, with an ellipse for each land use.

# Colours for each site and each land use
site_col <- c("Conv_agri" = "bisque", "Org_agri" = "bisque3",
              "Grass" = "orange",
              "Oak_20" = "darkolivegreen1", "Oak_28" = "darkolivegreen2",
              "Oak_33" = "darkolivegreen3", "Oak_44" = "palegreen3",
              "Oak_51" = "darkolivegreen4", "Oak_54" = "darkolivegreen",
              "Oak_ref" = "turquoise4")
land_use_col <- c("Conventional agriculture" = "bisque",
                  "Organic agriculture" = "bisque3",
                  "Grassland" = "orange",
                  "Oak" = "darkolivegreen2",
                  "Old Ref" = "turquoise4")

#   - physeq: the phyloseq object used for the distances (for the metadata)
#   - pcoa: the result of ordinate()
#   - title: the title of the plot
plot_pcoa <- function(physeq, pcoa, title) {
  # Sample scores on the first two axes, with the metadata of the samples
  scores <- plot_ordination(physeq, pcoa, justDF = TRUE)
  # Variation explained by the first two axes, for the axis labels
  var_expl <- round(100 * pcoa$values$Relative_eig[1:2], 1)

  ggplot(scores, aes(x = Axis.1, y = Axis.2)) +
    stat_ellipse(aes(fill = Land_use), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = SiteID), size = 2.5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = site_col, breaks = names(site_col)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = land_use_col) +
    labs(title = title,
         x = paste0("Axis 1 (", var_expl[1], "%)"),
         y = paste0("Axis 2 (", var_expl[2], "%)"),
         colour = "Site", fill = "Land use") +
    coord_fixed() +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
}


p_pcoa_bray <- plot_pcoa(otu_table_hel, pcoa_bray,
                         "Bray-Curtis (Hellinger, rarefied)")
p_pcoa_bray









p_pcoa_ait <- plot_pcoa(otu_table_clr, pcoa_ait,
                        "Aitchison (CLR, non-rarefied)")
p_pcoa_ait









p_pcoa_jac <- plot_pcoa(otu_table_rarefy, pcoa_jac,
                        "Jaccard (presence-absence, rarefied)")
p_pcoa_jac










Compare the distance metrics

p_pcoa_all <- ggarrange(p_pcoa_bray, p_pcoa_ait, p_pcoa_jac,
                        ncol = 3, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "right")
p_pcoa_all








In the three PCoAs, the first axis separates the agricultural sites from the grassland and the forests: this is the largest difference in the fungal communities. Conventional and organic agriculture overlap. With Bray-Curtis and Jaccard, the old reference forest (Oak_ref) is clearly separated from the oak plantations (only one sample of Oak_51 lies close to it). With Aitchison, the samples of the reference forest are spread along the second axis, and their ellipse overlaps with the plantations.
The metrics therefore lead to different conclusions about how similar the plantations are to the reference forest. Which one to use? The Jaccard distances only use presence-absence, and show the same separation as Bray-Curtis: the plantations and the reference forest differ in which OTUs are present, not only in their abundances. With the Aitchison distance, a pseudocount is added to all counts before the log-ratio transformation, so absent OTUs and OTUs with very few reads get similar values. This can blur the differences caused by OTUs that are present in one group and absent in the other.

title: Beta diversity
text:
PERMANOVA
The PCoA shows the patterns, but does not test them. The permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) tests whether the centroids (multivariate means) of groups of samples differ[3]. vegan::adonis2() calculates a pseudo-F ratio, similar to the F ratio of an ANOVA, and compares it with the values obtained after randomly permuting the samples between groups. The null hypothesis is H0: the centroids of all groups are equivalent.

Site and land use
We first test site and land use in the same model, each one after the other (by = "margin").

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ SiteID + Land_use, data = meta_rare,
        permutations = 999, by = "margin")

Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
Marginal effects of terms
Permutation: free
Number of permutations: 999

adonis2(formula = dist_bray ~ SiteID + Land_use, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999, by = "margin")

SiteID    5   3.9999 0.13398 3.6386  0.001 ***
Land_use  0   0.0000 0.00000   -Inf           
Residual 77  16.9291 0.56705                  
Total    86  29.8547 1.00000                  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Land use has 0 degrees of freedom and no F value. Why? Look at the metadata:

table(meta_rare$SiteID, meta_rare$Land_use)

           
            Conventional agriculture Organic agriculture Grassland Oak Old Ref
  Conv_agri                        9                   0         0   0       0
  Grass                            0                   0         9   0       0
  Oak_20                           0                   0         0   7       0
  Oak_28                           0                   0         0   8       0
  Oak_33                           0                   0         0   8       0
  Oak_44                           0                   0         0   9       0
  Oak_51                           0                   0         0  10       0
  Oak_54                           0                   0         0   9       0
  Oak_ref                          0                   0         0   0       9
  Org_agri                         0                   9         0   0       0


Each site belongs to a single land use: SiteID is nested within Land_use. Once the sites are in the model, land use cannot explain anything more: the two variables are redundant. We therefore test each variable alone.

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ SiteID, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)

Model     9   12.926 0.43295 6.5323  0.001 ***
Residual 77   16.929 0.56705                  
Total    86   29.855 1.00000                  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)

Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
Permutation: free
Number of permutations: 999

adonis2(formula = dist_bray ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)
         Df SumOfSqs      R2      F Pr(>F)    
Model     4   8.9257 0.29897 8.7428  0.001 ***
Residual 82  20.9290 0.70103                  
Total    86  29.8547 1.00000                  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Both site and land use are significantly associated with the composition of the fungal communities (p = 0.001, the smallest p-value possible with 999 permutations). Sites explain 43% of the variation (R2 = 0.43), land use 30% (R2 = 0.30). Sites explain more because they include the land use and the differences between the sites of the same land use (e.g., plantations of different ages).
With by = "terms", the variables are tested in sequence: each term only gets the variation not explained by the terms before it. Land use first, then the differences between the sites of the same land use:

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ Land_use + SiteID, data = meta_rare,
        permutations = 999, by = "terms")

         Df SumOfSqs      R2       F Pr(>F)    
Land_use  4   8.9257 0.29897 10.1494  0.001 ***
SiteID    5   3.9999 0.13398  3.6386  0.001 ***
Residual 77  16.9291 0.56705                   
Total    86  29.8547 1.00000                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Land use explains 30% of the variation, and the sites explain another 13% within land uses: 30% + 13% = the 43% explained by the sites alone.


Compare the distance metrics
Is the effect of land use the same with the three distance metrics? The Aitchison distances include the two samples removed by rarefaction, so they use the metadata of all samples.

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_ait ~ Land_use, data = meta_all, permutations = 999)

Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
Permutation: free
Number of permutations: 999

Model     4    20390 0.28477 8.361  0.001 ***
Residual 84    51212 0.71523                 
Total    88    71602 1.00000

adonis2(dist_jac ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)

Permutation: free
Number of permutations: 999

adonis2(formula = dist_jac ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999)
         Df SumOfSqs      R2      F Pr(>F)    
Model     4    6.635 0.18812 4.7501  0.001 ***
Residual 82   28.634 0.81188                  
Total    86   35.269 1.00000                  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Land use is significant with the three metrics, and explains a similar part of the variation with Bray-Curtis (R2 = 0.30) and Aitchison (R2 = 0.28), but less with Jaccard (R2 = 0.19). Presence-absence gives the same weight to all OTUs: the many rare OTUs, found by chance in only a few samples, add variation that is not related to land use.


Soil properties
We can also test the effect of soil properties. Samples of the same land use are not independent. With the strata argument, the samples are only permuted within each land use (similar to a random factor in mixed models), so the test asks whether pH and phosphate explain the composition within land uses.

set.seed(100)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ pH + PO4, data = meta_rare, permutations = 999,
        by = "margin", strata = meta_rare$Land_use)

Both pH (R2 = 0.13) and phosphate (R2 = 0.03) are significant (p = 0.001).






Note



strata only changes how the samples are permuted, not the R2, which is still calculated on the total variation. pH differs strongly between land uses, so part of its R2 may also reflect the effect of land use.

title: Beta diversity
text:
Homogeneity of group dispersions
Homogeneity of the dispersions is not an assumption of PERMANOVA, but it affects its results: a significant PERMANOVA can be caused by differences in the spread of the samples within groups (dispersion), not only by different centroids. vegan::betadisper(), a multivariate analogue of Levene’s test[4], calculates the distance of each sample to the centroid of its group. We then test whether these distances differ between groups.

# Bray-Curtis
disp_bray <- betadisper(dist_bray, meta_rare$SiteID)
anova(disp_bray)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: Distances
          Df  Sum Sq  Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
Groups     9 0.38709 0.043010  19.862 < 2.2e-16 ***
Residuals 77 0.16674 0.002165                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

# Aitchison
disp_ait <- betadisper(dist_ait, meta_all$SiteID)
anova(disp_ait)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: Distances
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
Groups     9 1376.1 152.903  12.021 1.004e-11 ***
Residuals 79 1004.8  12.719                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



Plot

# Distance to the centroid of each sample, for both metrics
disp_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(meta_rare[, c("SiteID", "Land_use")],
             distance = disp_bray$distances, metric = "Bray-Curtis"),
  data.frame(meta_all[, c("SiteID", "Land_use")],
             distance = disp_ait$distances, metric = "Aitchison"))
disp_df$metric <- factor(disp_df$metric, levels = c("Bray-Curtis", "Aitchison"))

# Order the sites by land use for the plot
disp_df$SiteID <- factor(disp_df$SiteID,
                         levels = unique(disp_df$SiteID[order(disp_df$Land_use,
                                                              disp_df$SiteID)]))

p_disp <- ggplot(disp_df, aes(x = SiteID, y = distance)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = Land_use), outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(size = 1, width = 0.1, height = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = land_use_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Distance to the site centroid", fill = "Land use") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
p_disp








The dispersions differ significantly between sites with both metrics (Bray-Curtis: F = 19.9, p < 0.001; Aitchison: F = 12.0, p < 0.001). The boxplots show that the agricultural samples have a lower dispersion than the other sites: their communities are more homogeneous (with Aitchison, also the youngest plantation, Oak_20). The reference forest has one of the highest dispersions. Part of the significant PERMANOVA may therefore be due to differences in dispersion, although the PCoA also shows a clear separation of the groups.


Without the agricultural sites
Do the other sites have similar dispersions? We remove the agricultural samples from the distance matrix and test again.

keep <- !meta_rare$Land_use %in% c("Conventional agriculture",
                                   "Organic agriculture")
dist_bray_noagri <- as.dist(as.matrix(dist_bray)[keep, keep])
disp_bray_noagri <- betadisper(dist_bray_noagri, meta_rare$SiteID[keep])
anova(disp_bray_noagri)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: Distances
          Df   Sum Sq   Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)   
Groups     7 0.065613 0.0093732  3.5784 0.002737 **
Residuals 61 0.159782 0.0026194                    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Without the agricultural sites, the dispersions still differ between sites (F = 3.6, p = 0.003), but much less: the differences in dispersion are mainly due to the agricultural sites. Among the other sites, Oak_51 and Oak_ref are the most dispersed.
